metadata.name: bedrock-agentcore-control
metadata.overview:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Control is the management interface for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform for building, deploying, and operating AI agents. Administrators and developers use it to configure the resources that agents depend on, without managing underlying infrastructure.

Teams use it to set up isolated hosting for agent code, managed conversational memory, and gateways that expose APIs as agent tools. They also configure agent identities and credentials, deterministic rules that govern tool use, sandboxed code and browser environments, and quality evaluations.

The service works with any agent framework and foundation model. It helps organizations apply network isolation, encryption, fine-grained access control, and centralized monitoring as agents move from prototype to production.
useCases: Deploying production AI agents built with open-source frameworks such as LangGraph, CrewAI, or Strands Agents into isolated serverless sessions for customer support, workflow automation, data analysis, or coding assistance.

Turning existing internal APIs, serverless functions, and OpenAPI-described services into governed agent tools behind a single gateway, with centralized authentication, web-application firewall protection, and deterministic policy checks on every tool call.

Building an internal agent platform that gives development teams approved tools, shared memory stores, managed agent identities, a curated catalog of agents and tools, and centralized observability and compliance controls.

Letting agents act on behalf of signed-in end users with third-party services such as Slack, GitHub, Salesforce, or Google Workspace through managed OAuth and API key credential handling, without exposing secrets in agent code.

Running long-lived, multi-agent, or GPU-accelerated agent workloads on managed compute inside the organization's own account and private network, while continuously evaluating agent quality against live traffic.

relationshipToOtherNamespaces.relationship: Companion data plane. This control plane creates and configures runtimes, gateways, memories, tools, identities, payments and evaluators that are invoked through the bedrock-agentcore data plane (InvokeAgentRuntime, InvokeGateway, memory events/records, browser and code interpreter sessions, workload access tokens). Both planes share the bedrock-agentcore IAM action prefix.

Successor control plane for AWS Agent Registry. The Registry and RegistryRecord operations in bedrock-agentcore-control are legacy and shut down on October 30, 2026; agent-registry-control owns the AWS::AgentRegistry CloudFormation types (create handlers use agent-registry:CreateRegistry).

Successor data plane for AWS Agent Registry discovery and search (agent-registry IAM prefix, agent-registry.amazonaws.com service principal) replacing registry access through the bedrock-agentcore namespaces.

Agent runtime and harness execution roles invoke Amazon Bedrock foundation models; Bedrock models power memory extraction strategies, LLM-as-a-judge evaluators and natural-language policy authoring; Bedrock Guardrails can be referenced from AgentCore policies.

Agents for Amazon Bedrock is the earlier managed agent offering that AgentCore is positioned as an enhanced alternative to; AgentCore Gateway also offers a managed Bedrock Knowledge Bases connector target.

Execution roles for runtimes, harnesses, gateways, browsers, code interpreters and memory; capacity provider operator role and instance profile; iam:PassRole on create; five AgentCore service-linked roles (Network, RuntimeIdentity, GatewayNetwork, Identity, RuntimeInstances).
The bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com service principal assumes customer execution roles via sts:AssumeRole; trust policies should use aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount to prevent confused deputy.

Customer managed keys for gateways, memories, policy engines, the token vault and capacity provider EBS volumes (default is AWS owned keys); asymmetric KMS keys sign private_key_jwt client assertions for OAuth2 credential providers.

Stores OAuth2 client secrets (service-managed or customer-managed), credential provider secrets, payment wallet credentials, and certificates referenced by browsers, code interpreters and gateway targets.
Container images for agent runtimes and custom harness environments are pulled from Amazon ECR; ECR VPC endpoints are required for VPC-mode container agents without internet access.

Direct code deployment artifacts, browser session recordings, browser enterprise policies, gateway tool schemas, harness skills and self-managed memory payload delivery use S3; the service also stores data at rest in S3.
Amazon EFS access points can be mounted into agent runtimes, browsers and code interpreters over NFS (TCP 2049) as bring-your-own persistent file systems.
Amazon S3 Files access points can be mounted into runtimes, harnesses, browsers and code interpreters as shared file systems.

VPC-mode resources create ENIs in customer subnets with customer security groups; the Instances compute type launches EC2 managed instances in the customer account from a capacity provider; interface VPC endpoints (PrivateLink) provide private API access.

Capacity providers define root, ephemeral and persistent EBS volumes (optionally encrypted with customer managed KMS keys) that are attached to instance-backed agent sessions and persist across session stops.
Gateway targets, JWT authorizers and OAuth2 credential providers can reach private endpoints and private identity providers through managed or self-managed VPC Lattice resource configurations.
Lambda functions serve as gateway MCP targets, gateway request/response interceptors, harness lifecycle hook targets, and code-based evaluators.
Amazon API Gateway REST API stages can be added as gateway targets and exposed to agents as MCP tools.
SNS topics receive self-managed memory strategy job notifications (including cross-account topics) and harness lifecycle hook events.
EventBridge receives registry approval/lifecycle notifications and can be a harness lifecycle hook target.
Memory record streaming publishes memory record create/update/delete events (optionally with full record text) to Kinesis Data Streams, including cross-account streams.
Built-in metrics and GenAI observability dashboards for runtimes, gateways, memory, tools, identity and policy; AWS WAF gateway metrics (WafBlocks, WafFailOpens, WafFailCloses).
Vended log delivery for runtime, memory, gateway, built-in tools and identity resources; runtime command audit logs; online evaluations sample agent traces from CloudWatch Logs.
Spans and traces are delivered through CloudWatch Transaction Search / X-Ray trace segment destinations.
Control-plane operations are recorded as management events; data events such as InvokeGateway and runtime invocations are logged when explicitly enabled with advanced event selectors.
Amazon Cognito user pools are the default JWT inbound authorizer created by the console/CLI and a supported OAuth2 credential provider vendor.
Regional AWS WAF web ACLs can be associated with gateways to inspect inbound requests, with FAIL_CLOSE (default) or FAIL_OPEN failure modes.
AWS RAM shares registries cross-account using AgentCore registry managed permissions (read-only, consumer, publisher, admin).

Service control policies use AgentCore condition keys (authorizer type, KMS key, policy engine, VPC subnets) to enforce organizational guardrails; RAM organization sharing auto-accepts registry shares.
Harnesses can be invoked from AWS Step Functions workflows through an InvokeHarness state.
AgentCore Gateway integrates with AWS Certificate Manager (for example, for custom domain names).
The service stores customer data and metadata at rest in Amazon DynamoDB (service-managed), encrypted with AWS owned or customer managed keys.
The AgentCore CLI uses AWS CodeBuild projects to build and push agent container images during deployment.

entities.name: AgentRuntime
entities.overview:
An agent runtime is a managed hosting environment for an AI agent or tool built with any framework or foundation model. You package your code as a container image or code bundle. The service runs it on demand and handles scaling and infrastructure management.

Each user session runs in its own isolated micro virtual machine with dedicated CPU, memory, and file system. When a session ends, its environment is terminated and memory is sanitized. This helps keep conversation context and agent state separated between users. Sessions can stay active for hours to support long-running and asynchronous work.

You decide how callers authenticate, using AWS credentials or tokens from your own identity provider. You also choose whether the agent reaches resources over public networking or through your virtual private cloud. Configuration changes are saved as immutable versions to support controlled rollouts and rollback.

entities.name: AgentRuntimeEndpoint
entities.overview:
An agent runtime endpoint is a named, stable access point that routes invocations to a specific version of an AgentCore Runtime. Each runtime receives a default endpoint that automatically follows the newest version. You can add named endpoints for environments such as development, staging, and production.

Because runtime versions are immutable, endpoints help you promote, test, and roll back agent changes without changing how callers reach the agent. You can repoint a named endpoint to another version without downtime, while other endpoints keep serving their current versions.

Endpoints also serve as an access-control point. You can tag an endpoint and attach a resource-based policy to it, including policies that grant cross-account or network-restricted access. Invocation requests are evaluated against the policies of both the endpoint and its parent runtime.

entities.name: ApiKeyCredentialProvider
entities.overview:
An API key credential provider stores an API key that your AI agents use to authenticate with external services and third-party APIs. It helps keep sensitive keys out of agent code, prompts, and configuration files.

You can let the service create and manage the backing secret, or reference your own AWS Secrets Manager secret. Referencing your own secret lets you control its encryption key, rotation schedule, tags, and access policy. When the external service rotates its key, you can replace the stored value, and agents use the new key on later requests.

Agents and gateways retrieve the key at runtime by presenting a workload identity token and passing IAM authorization checks. Gateways can attach the key to outbound tool requests as a header or query parameter, which helps keep it out of agent code.

entities.name: Browser
entities.overview:
A browser is a managed, cloud-based web browser environment that AI agents use to interact with websites and web applications. Agents can navigate pages, fill out forms, click elements, capture screenshots, and extract content without running browser infrastructure themselves.

Each browser defines how its sessions behave. You can choose public internet access or connectivity through your own virtual private cloud. You can also assign an IAM execution role and record sessions to Amazon S3 for replay and auditing. Optional settings apply enterprise browser policies, trust private certificate authorities, and mount shared file systems. Request signing can identify agent traffic to participating websites, which helps reduce CAPTCHA challenges.

Sessions started from a browser run in isolated environments that are terminated and cleaned up when they end. Live viewing lets people watch or take over a session in real time, which helps with troubleshooting and human-in-the-loop workflows.

entities.name: BrowserProfile
entities.overview:
A browser profile in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser stores browser state, such as cookies and local storage, captured from a browser session. New sessions can start from that saved state, so they begin where an earlier session left off.

This helps AI agents continue authenticated or multi-step web workflows without signing in again or rebuilding context each time. Common uses include persistent logins, preserving shopping carts or form progress, and automating tasks on sites that require sign-in.

State is captured only when a session is explicitly saved to the profile, and each save replaces the previously stored state. Running sessions keep the state they started with, and later saves apply only to new sessions. Because profiles can hold sensitive authentication cookies, access to them is typically restricted with IAM policies.

entities.name: CapacityProvider
entities.overview:
A capacity provider defines the Amazon EC2 infrastructure that Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime uses for the Instances compute type. It specifies the operating system, allowed instance types, VPC placement, storage volumes, and the IAM roles used to operate the instances. A single capacity provider is reusable across multiple agent runtimes.

AgentCore provisions, patches, scales, and tears down these instances inside your own AWS account as EC2 managed instances. This model helps keep agent data in your account and lets your existing account controls govern the instances, network interfaces, and volumes. Idle timeout and maximum lifetime settings help stop idle or long-running instances automatically.

Capacity providers suit agents that need sessions lasting up to 14 days, GPU or accelerator hardware, or several collaborating agents on one host. Named persistent EBS volumes retain workspace data across session restarts. Volume encryption can follow the account's EBS encryption settings or use a customer managed AWS KMS key.

entities.name: CodeInterpreter
entities.overview:
A code interpreter gives AI agents a managed, sandboxed environment for writing, running, and debugging code. It helps agents perform precise calculations, data analysis, file processing, and visualization tasks that are difficult to solve through reasoning alone.

Each code interpreter defines how its sessions behave. Settings include network access, an IAM role for reaching AWS resources, trusted certificate authorities, and mounted shared file systems. Sessions run in isolated environments with dedicated compute, memory, and storage, and are terminated when they end.

You can start with a managed default configuration or define your own. Custom configurations support sandboxed, public internet, or private VPC connectivity to help meet enterprise security requirements.

entities.name: ConfigurationBundle
entities.overview:
A configuration bundle holds the dynamic settings an AgentCore agent reads at runtime, such as system prompts, model IDs, and tool descriptions. It separates agent behavior from agent code, so teams can adjust how an agent responds without redeploying it.

Each change produces a new immutable version linked to its parent, similar to commits in a source control system. Branches keep experimental lineages apart from the main line. Teams can review history, compare versions, and roll back by referencing an earlier version.

Bundles support a continuous improvement loop for agent quality. A gateway can apply a chosen bundle version to matching traffic, or split traffic between two versions for A/B testing. Optimization recommendations can write improved prompts or tool descriptions back as new versions. Bundle content can optionally be encrypted with a customer managed key.

entities.name: ConsentPortal
entities.overview:
A consent portal is an AWS-hosted web experience where end users grant an agent permission to access external services on their behalf. Users sign in through your organization's OpenID Connect identity provider, review the available service connections, and approve each one individually.

The portal presents the OAuth connections configured on an agent gateway. It trusts the same identity provider that the gateway uses to authenticate callers. The portal is designed to run the OAuth authorization flow server-side, keeping access tokens out of the user's browser.

It binds each approval to the signed-in user, which helps ensure the person who started an authorization is the one who completed it. The resulting tokens are stored per user in AgentCore Identity, so agents can reuse them in later tool calls without repeated consent prompts. This replaces the custom callback and session-binding application that teams would otherwise build and host.

entities.name: Dataset
entities.overview:
A dataset is a managed collection of test scenarios used to evaluate AI agents built with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Each scenario records the inputs sent to an agent and optional ground truth, such as expected responses, tool sequences, and assertions.

Datasets help teams keep evaluation inputs steady while their agents change. You refine scenarios in an editable draft, then publish the draft as a numbered version that can't be changed. Evaluations pinned to a published version reuse the same scenarios, which helps make score comparisons meaningful for regression testing and deployment gates.

Each example is checked against the schema chosen when the dataset is created, so malformed scenarios are rejected when they are added. A scenario can script fixed conversation turns or describe a simulated user persona with a goal. Stored content is encrypted at rest, and you can choose a customer managed key for more control.

entities.name: DatasetExample
entities.overview:
A dataset example is a single evaluation scenario stored in an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore dataset. Each example describes a conversation used to test an agent, either as scripted user turns or as a simulated user persona with a goal.

Examples can carry ground truth such as expected responses, expected tool sequences, and natural language assertions. Evaluators use this ground truth to score agent behavior against known expectations.

You add, revise, and remove examples in the dataset's editable draft, and each change is checked against the dataset's declared schema. Publishing the draft captures its examples in an immutable numbered version, which helps keep regression tests and deployment gates stable. The draft stays editable for further changes.

entities.name: Evaluator
entities.overview:
An evaluator defines how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations scores the quality of an AI agent. It assesses agent behavior for a single tool call, a request-response trace, or a full conversation session.

Custom evaluators let you apply domain-specific quality standards. You can write judging instructions and a rating scale for a chosen language model, or supply your own AWS Lambda function. Code-based evaluators suit deterministic checks such as schema validation or business rule enforcement. You can also run an existing built-in or third-party evaluator's logic on your own model.

Evaluators help teams test agents during development, gate deployments, and monitor production quality over time. You can encrypt evaluator instructions and rating scales with your own AWS KMS key.

entities.name: Gateway
entities.overview:
An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway gives AI agents one managed endpoint for reaching tools, other agents, and large language models. It turns existing APIs, serverless functions, and remote tool servers into Model Context Protocol tools that agents can discover and call.

The gateway can authenticate and authorize callers with OAuth tokens or AWS credentials before forwarding their requests. It then supplies the credentials each backend requires, so agents do not need to hold those secrets directly. Optional features add policy-based authorization, custom request and response processing, web traffic filtering, and natural-language tool search.

Because the gateway is fully managed and scales automatically, teams can centralize tool access and governance without running proxy infrastructure. Customer-managed key encryption, metrics, and optional logging help support security and audit requirements.

entities.name: GatewayRateLimit
entities.overview:
A gateway rate limit defines throttling rules for traffic that flows through an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway. It caps request rates, model token consumption, and concurrent connections for the tools, models, and agents behind the gateway.

Each rate limit groups traffic into buckets using ordered dimensions, such as target, tool, model, authenticated caller identity, or selected request attributes. Entries assign allowed rates to specific values or to a wildcard default, with the most specific match taking precedence.

Rate limits help protect downstream services from traffic spikes, distribute capacity fairly across tenants and users, and contain runaway agent consumption. They complement, rather than replace, authentication, authorization, and web application firewall protections.

entities.name: GatewayRule
entities.overview:
A gateway rule tells an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway how to handle requests that match specific criteria. Each rule belongs to one gateway and has a priority, optional conditions, and one or two actions.

Conditions can match the calling IAM principal, the request path, or the requested model. Actions can route traffic to a chosen target, split traffic between two targets, or apply a configuration bundle version. For inference traffic, a rule can also define fallback destinations to try when the primary target fails.

The gateway evaluates rules in priority order and applies the first match for each action type. Rules help teams run A/B tests and canary releases, pin testers to specific configurations, and set default routing without redeploying targets.

entities.name: GatewayTarget
entities.overview:
A gateway target defines a backend that an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway connects to on behalf of AI agents. It can front tools such as AWS Lambda functions, REST APIs, and MCP servers, plus other agents and model providers. Each target pairs a backend endpoint with the outbound credentials the gateway uses, such as its service role, OAuth tokens, or stored API keys.

Targets help teams expose existing services to agents without rewriting them. The gateway translates agent requests into calls the backend understands, or forwards traffic directly where translation is not needed. Targets can reach private resources in a VPC, trust private certificate authorities, and limit which request headers and query parameters pass through.

For tool backends, the gateway can discover and cache available tools, prompts, and resources, and refresh that catalog when the backend changes. This is designed to give agents one consistent, governed entry point to many tools.

entities.name: Harness
entities.overview:
A harness is a managed agent definition in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. You declare the model, instructions, tools, skills, memory, and execution limits, and AgentCore runs the agent loop for you. Changing a model or adding a tool becomes a configuration change rather than a code rewrite.

Each session runs in its own isolated microVM with a filesystem and shell. The agent can write and run code and call tools through gateways, MCP servers, a browser, or a code interpreter. It can also retain short-term and long-term memory across sessions.

A harness runs with an IAM role you own and can connect to your VPC. Callers authenticate with IAM credentials or tokens from a trusted identity provider. Each configuration update creates an immutable version, which helps you promote or roll back changes in a controlled way. Agent activity is traced to Amazon CloudWatch for troubleshooting.

entities.name: HarnessEndpoint
entities.overview:
A harness endpoint is a named, stable entry point for invoking a specific version of an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness. Callers target the endpoint by name, so the version behind it can change without changing how the agent is called.

Each harness has a default endpoint that automatically follows the newest version. You can add named endpoints, such as development, staging, or production, that stay pinned to a chosen version. To promote a tested version or roll back to an earlier one, you repoint the endpoint.

This helps teams roll out agent changes in stages and recover quickly when a new version misbehaves. IAM permissions can scope who manages or invokes each endpoint separately.

entities.name: Memory
entities.overview:
An AgentCore memory gives AI agents a managed place to keep conversation history and learned context. It helps agents stay coherent within a conversation and personalize interactions across separate sessions.

Short-term memory records each interaction as timestamped events grouped by user and session. Long-term memory uses configurable strategies to extract durable insights, such as facts, preferences, summaries, and episodes. These insights are organized under hierarchical namespaces that support scoped retrieval and access control.

You control how long raw events and extracted records are retained, and you can encrypt stored data with your own KMS key. A memory can also stream record changes to your own data streams or hand conversations to your own extraction pipelines.

entities.name: Oauth2CredentialProvider
entities.overview:
An OAuth2 credential provider holds the client credentials and endpoint settings for an external OAuth 2.0 authorization server. AgentCore Identity uses it to obtain access tokens so agents can call third-party services and internal APIs. Preconfigured settings cover popular services such as Google, GitHub, Slack, and Salesforce. A custom configuration works with other OAuth 2.0-compatible servers through discovery or manually entered endpoints.

The provider supports machine-to-machine access, user-delegated access with explicit consent, and on-behalf-of token exchange for users who are already signed in. Obtained tokens are stored in the token vault and returned to authorized agents, which helps keep long-term secrets out of agent code.

You can let the service manage the client secret or reference your own AWS Secrets Manager secret. To avoid shared secrets, the provider can instead sign client assertions with an AWS KMS asymmetric key. It can also reach identity providers hosted inside your VPC through private connectivity.

entities.name: OnlineEvaluationConfig
entities.overview:
An online evaluation configuration continuously assesses the quality of an AI agent running in production. It samples completed agent sessions from the agent's telemetry in Amazon CloudWatch Logs and scores them with selected evaluators. Evaluation runs asynchronously alongside live traffic and is designed not to add latency to user responses.

You choose the log groups and service names that identify the agent, the sampling rate, optional filters, and a session idle timeout. Evaluators can be built-in, third-party, or your own model-based or code-based judges.

The service runs evaluations under an IAM role that you provide and writes results to CloudWatch log groups and metrics. This helps teams track quality trends, alarm on regressions, and pause or resume monitoring without redeploying the agent.

entities.name: PaymentConnector
entities.overview:
A payment connector links your AgentCore payments configuration to an external wallet provider, such as Coinbase Developer Platform or Stripe with Privy. It lets agents sign payments for paid APIs, MCP servers, and web content through that provider's wallet infrastructure.

Connectors reference provider credentials held in a managed credential store instead of embedding secrets. This design helps keep provider API keys and wallet secrets out of agent code and runtime environments.

You can supply credentials you created with the provider. For Coinbase, you can instead complete a one-time consent flow so the service provisions credentials for you. Service-provisioned credentials can be replaced on demand, which helps support routine rotation and response to suspected exposure.

entities.name: PaymentCredentialProvider
entities.overview:
A payment credential provider stores the credentials that AgentCore payments uses to work with an external wallet provider. Supported providers include Coinbase Developer Platform and Stripe with Privy. The provider keeps API keys, app secrets, wallet secrets, and authorization keys in AWS Secrets Manager rather than in agent code.

At runtime, the payments service uses these stored credentials to obtain short-lived authentication tokens and signatures for wallet operations. This design keeps raw secrets away from agents, which helps reduce the risk of exposing credentials through prompts or code.

You can let the service manage the underlying secrets or reference secrets you already govern in Secrets Manager. Referencing your own secrets helps you apply existing encryption, rotation, tagging, and access policies. You can replace stored values when you rotate credentials with the wallet provider.

entities.name: PaymentManager
entities.overview:
A payment manager coordinates how your AI agents pay for APIs, MCP servers, and web content on behalf of end users. It serves as the configuration and authorization boundary for agent payment activity in an account and Region.

Callers authenticate with either AWS IAM credentials or bearer tokens from an OpenID Connect identity provider. Token validation can restrict access by audience, client, scope, and custom claims.

The payment manager assumes an IAM service role to retrieve wallet provider credentials at runtime, helping keep raw keys out of agent code. Data is encrypted at rest by default, and you can supply a customer managed key for sensitive fields. You can create separate payment managers to organize payment activity by application, environment, or team.

entities.name: Policy
entities.overview:
A policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an authorization rule that governs how AI agents use tools exposed through AgentCore Gateway. Each policy belongs to a policy engine and is written in Cedar or in Dogwood, a Cedar-compatible language.

Policies specify which callers can invoke which tools on which gateway, and under what conditions. Conditions can examine tool input values, caller identity claims, guardrail content-safety scores, and earlier actions within the same session.

When its policy engine is attached to a gateway, each tool request is evaluated outside the agent's code before access is granted. Requests are denied unless a policy permits them, and a matching forbid rule overrides any permit. A policy can also run in an observe-only mode that records its would-be decisions without affecting traffic. This helps teams validate new rules before enforcing them.

entities.name: PolicyEngine
entities.overview:
A policy engine stores authorization policies that govern what AI agents can do with their tools. When attached to one or more gateways, it evaluates each agent tool call and returns an allow or deny decision before the tool runs.

Policies in an engine apply across every attached gateway wherever a request matches their scope. Requests are denied unless a policy permits them, and any matching forbid rule overrides permits. Decisions can be observed without blocking traffic, which helps teams validate rules before enforcing them.

Because enforcement happens outside agent code, it helps rules apply consistently regardless of how an agent is built or prompted. The engine can also track actions within a session to support sequencing, counting, and budget rules. Policy data is encrypted at rest, with an optional customer managed key selected at creation.

entities.name: PolicyGeneration
entities.overview:
A policy generation converts plain-English authorization requirements into candidate policies for a Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policy engine. It helps teams define which agent tool calls are allowed without first learning a formal policy language.

Each generation draws on the policy engine and the tool definitions of an associated AgentCore gateway. The service translates the description into one or more candidate statements, each linked to the part of the text it covers. Every candidate is checked against the gateway's tool schema. Automated reasoning then flags rules that look overly permissive, overly restrictive, or ineffective.

Generation runs asynchronously, and candidates remain available for seven days before automatic removal. Candidates are not enforced until they are added to the policy engine as policies. Testing them in log-only mode first helps confirm their effect on real traffic.

entities.name: Registry
entities.overview:
A registry is a centralized catalog for organizing and discovering MCP servers, agents, agent skills, and custom resources across your organization. It helps teams find and reuse approved tools and agents instead of rebuilding them. It also gives administrators one place to govern which resources builders can discover.

Each registry has its own name, description, consumer authorization settings, and record approval settings. Consumers authorize with AWS IAM credentials or with JSON Web Tokens issued by a corporate identity provider. Approval settings determine whether submitted entries need curator review before they become discoverable.

You can create separate registries by team, resource type, or development stage. Humans and AI agents search approved entries using hybrid semantic and keyword search, directly or through an MCP-compatible endpoint.

entities.name: RegistryRecord
entities.overview:
A registry record describes one AI resource in an AWS Agent Registry catalog. The resource can be an MCP server with its tools, an Agent-to-Agent (A2A) agent, an agent skill, or a custom resource. Each record holds the resource's name, version, description, and protocol-specific descriptor content. This metadata helps people and AI agents find existing resources and understand how to use them.

Records follow a governed lifecycle. Publishers draft and refine a record, then submit it for review. Curators approve or reject it, or retire it permanently through deprecation. Registry search and the registry's MCP endpoint are designed to return only approved records to consumers. Edits to an approved record create a new draft, while the approved version stays discoverable until the update is approved.

Records for MCP servers and A2A agents can be populated from a live HTTPS endpoint. When the endpoint is protected, the registry authenticates with an OAuth credential provider or an IAM role. Synchronization helps keep catalog entries aligned with the resources they describe.

entities.name: TokenVault
entities.overview:
The token vault is the managed credential store behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. It holds OAuth 2.0 access and refresh tokens, OAuth client credentials, and API keys that agents use to reach external tools and services. Each account uses a default vault in each AWS Region.

The vault helps keep long-lived secrets out of agent code and configuration files. It is designed to bind stored user tokens to the specific agent and end user that obtained them. Retrieval is designed to require verifiable proof of the requesting agent's workload identity. Stored refresh tokens are reused automatically, which helps reduce repeated consent prompts for end users.

Vault data is encrypted at rest by default with an AWS owned key. You can instead select a customer managed AWS KMS key to control key policies, rotation, and deletion. Tags help you organize the vault and support tag-based access control in IAM policies.

entities.name: WorkloadIdentity
entities.overview:
A workload identity gives an AI agent or automated workload its own stable, verifiable identity within an AWS account and Region. Agents use it to authenticate as themselves instead of impersonating users, wherever the agent runs.

AgentCore creates workload identities automatically for agents hosted on its managed runtime and gateway. You can also create identities yourself for self-hosted, hybrid, or test deployments that need specific names. Every identity lives in a single agent identity directory for the account, which supports central governance and auditing.

A workload identity anchors how an agent obtains access tokens tied to itself and, when acting for someone, to that user. These tokens let the agent retrieve OAuth tokens and API keys from a managed token vault, helping avoid secrets in agent code. Each identity can also hold an allowlist of return URLs, helping keep user consent redirects bound to trusted applications.

mitigations.statement: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Control service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made against trusted resources or AWS service-owned resources

mitigationContext.context: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Control API calls from your VPCs can target AgentCore resources in another account. Restricting those calls to resources in your organization enforces the resource perimeter on your network.

mitigations.statement: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Control service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made by trusted identities or AWS services

mitigationContext.context: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Control API calls from your VPCs can be made by identities outside your organization. Restricting those calls to principals in your organization enforces the identity perimeter on your network.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime's execution role should be restricted to accessing resources only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: The `$.roleArn` request parameter designates your agent runtime's IAM execution role, and your agent or tool code calls AWS services with that role's credentials. Restricting those calls to expected networks enforces the network perimeter on your identities and helps prevent the use of those credentials from unexpected networks.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime's execution role should be assumed only by AgentCore acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Your agent runtime binds its IAM execution role through the `$.roleArn` request parameter, and the role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only AgentCore, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime should be accessed only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls to your agent runtime can originate from the internet and from your VPCs through an interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink), and your agent runtime's resource-based policy specifies which principals can invoke it. A network perimeter helps you confirm that your agent runtime can be accessed only from expected networks.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime resources

mitigationContext.context: Resource-based policies on an agent runtime and its endpoint in another account can grant your principals access to invoke that runtime. The resource perimeter helps restrict your identities to resources your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime should be in an Amazon VPC

mitigationContext.context: VPC network mode places elastic network interfaces for your agent runtime in the VPC subnets you specify, governed by the security groups you choose. Placing an agent runtime in a VPC is optional and enables network-level isolation and access controls.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime should have elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in more than one Availability Zone (AZ)

mitigationContext.context: On the default microVM compute type, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore creates elastic network interfaces for your agent runtime's VPC configuration in the `$.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.subnets[*]` subnets. Placing those network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone provides network-level redundancy and helps keep connectivity available when one zone is disrupted.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime's resource policy should limit permissions to a subset of IAM principals, rather than granting access to all IAM principals

mitigationContext.context: An agent runtime can carry its own resource-based policy that names the IAM principals allowed to perform invocation and session actions, set through `$.policy`. Requiring explicit principal definitions rather than wildcard principals helps prevent the agent runtime from inadvertently being made public or accessible to unintended actors. This mitigation applies to an agent runtime whose callers authenticate as IAM principals (SigV4). An agent runtime configured with OAuth (JWT) inbound authorization must name a wildcard principal instead, so this mitigation does not apply to it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime should only be configured with a trusted OpenID Connect identity provider

mitigationContext.context: An agent runtime sets its inbound JWT authorizer through `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl`, which can name OpenID Connect identity providers outside AWS. Restricting the inbound JWT authorizer helps keep the bearer tokens your agent runtime accepts flowing only from trusted targets.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime supports a resource-based policy that specifies who can access it and what actions they can perform. The identity perimeter helps restrict access to your agent runtimes to trusted identities and AWS services acting on your behalf.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime that uses an inbound JWT authorizer to authenticate principals should be configured only with trusted OIDC or OAuth 2.0 authorization server providers

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime can authenticate callers that invoke it with JWT bearer tokens from the OpenID Connect (OIDC) or OAuth 2.0 authorization server provider designated by `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl`, the provider's discovery URL. Configuring only trusted OIDC or OAuth 2.0 authorization server providers helps prevent an untrusted identity provider from being used to gain unintended access.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You can tag an agent runtime by calling `CreateAgentRuntime`, whose `$.tags{key}` request parameter carries a key-to-value map, or later by calling `TagResource`. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each agent runtime supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

mitigationContext.context: AgentCore attaches the security groups in `$.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.securityGroups[*]` to the elastic network interfaces it creates in your subnets in VPC network mode, and the groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` can replace your VPC's default security group on the managed VPC Lattice resource gateway that your inbound JWT authorizer uses to reach a private identity provider. Restricting the inbound and outbound rules to the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports helps reduce the network exposure of your agent runtime.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime should be configured to send application and trace logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery

mitigationContext.context: AgentCore Runtime produces application logs for each invocation of your agent runtime, recording the invocation's operation, request ID, session ID and request payload, and trace spans for each `InvokeAgentRuntime` call, recording the agent runtime, endpoint, session ID, latency and error type. Sending those logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery provides security-relevant visibility.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime endpoint should be accessed only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: Requests to your agent runtime endpoint can originate from any network, including unexpected networks, and are evaluated against the endpoint's own resource-based policy. A network perimeter helps you confirm that your agent runtime endpoint can be accessed only from expected networks.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime endpoint resources

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy on an agent runtime endpoint in another account can grant your principals access to invoke the runtime through that endpoint. That access also requires a matching grant in the resource-based policy on that runtime. The resource perimeter helps restrict your identities to resources your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime endpoint's resource policy should limit permissions to a subset of IAM principals, rather than granting access to all IAM principals

mitigationContext.context: An agent runtime endpoint can carry its own resource-based policy that names the IAM principals allowed to invoke the endpoint, set through `$.policy`. Requiring explicit principal definitions rather than wildcard principals helps prevent the agent runtime endpoint from inadvertently being made public or accessible to unintended actors. This mitigation applies to an agent runtime endpoint whose callers authenticate as IAM principals (SigV4). An agent runtime endpoint configured with OAuth (JWT) inbound authorization must name a wildcard principal instead, so this mitigation does not apply to it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime endpoint should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime endpoint supports a resource-based policy that specifies who can access it and what actions they can perform. The identity perimeter helps restrict access to your agent runtime endpoints to trusted identities and AWS services acting on your behalf.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime endpoint should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag an agent runtime endpoint through `$.tags{key}`, a key-to-value map on `CreateAgentRuntimeEndpoint`, or later by calling `TagResource`, separately from the agent runtime's tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each agent runtime endpoint supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API key credential provider should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag an API key credential provider through the `$.tags{key}` key-to-value map on `CreateApiKeyCredentialProvider` or later through `TagResource`, independently of your token vault's tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each API key credential provider supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API key credential provider should be configured to send TRACES logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery

mitigationContext.context: The TRACES spans that AgentCore Identity produces for your API key credential provider record each `GetResourceApiKey` retrieval with the requesting workload identity, the credential provider, the token vault and the error type. Sending those logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery provides security-relevant visibility.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore browser's execution role should be restricted to accessing resources only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: The `$.executionRoleArn` request parameter designates your custom browser's execution role, and code in each session's microVM can call AWS services with that role's credentials. Restricting those calls to expected networks enforces the network perimeter on your identities and helps prevent the use of those credentials from unexpected networks.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore browser's execution role should be assumed only by AgentCore acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: You can pass a custom browser's execution role through the `$.executionRoleArn` request parameter, and the role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only AgentCore, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore browser should be in an Amazon VPC

mitigationContext.context: Creating a custom browser in VPC network mode places elastic network interfaces for it in your VPC subnets with the security groups you specify. Placing a browser in a VPC is optional and enables network-level isolation and access controls.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore browser should have elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in more than one Availability Zone (AZ)

mitigationContext.context: For a custom browser in VPC mode, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore creates the browser's elastic network interfaces in the subnets from the `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.subnets[*]` subnet list. Placing those network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone provides network-level redundancy and helps keep connectivity available when one zone is disrupted.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore browser should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag a custom browser at creation through the `$.tags{key}` key-to-value map on `CreateBrowser`, or afterward through `TagResource`. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each browser supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore browser should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

mitigationContext.context: In VPC network mode, the security groups you specify in `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.securityGroups[*]` govern traffic on the elastic network interfaces that AgentCore creates for the browser. Restricting the inbound and outbound rules to the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports helps reduce the network exposure of your browser.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore browser profile should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You can tag your browser profile through the `$.tags{key}` map of tag keys to values when you call `CreateBrowserProfile`, or later by calling `TagResource`. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each browser profile supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider's default instance role, or instance profile where one is provided, should be restricted to accessing resources only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: The default instance role that AgentCore creates for your capacity provider, or the instance profile where the `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.launchTemplateSource.launchParameters.instanceProfileArn` request parameter designates one, is the role attached to every Amazon EC2 managed instance your capacity provider launches, whose credentials host processes and SSH sessions on those instances read from instance metadata to call AWS services, while your agent code uses the agent runtime execution role rather than this role. Restricting those calls to expected networks enforces the network perimeter on your identities and helps prevent the use of those credentials from unexpected networks.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider's infrastructure role should be assumed only by Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and its instance role only by Amazon EC2, acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: The `$.permissionsConfiguration.capacityProviderOperatorRoleArn` request parameter sets the infrastructure role that Amazon Bedrock AgentCore assumes, the `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.launchTemplateSource.launchParameters.instanceProfileArn` request parameter sets the instance profile whose instance role Amazon EC2 assumes, and each role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon EC2, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume those roles helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming them.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider's root volume, persistent volume, and ephemeral volume should have encryption at rest enabled

mitigationContext.context: When AgentCore creates volumes for your capacity provider's instances, the `CreateCapacityProvider` request parameters `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.rootVolume.encrypted` for the root volume, `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.volumes[*].ebsConfiguration.encrypted` for persistent volumes, and `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.launchTemplateSource.launchParameters.ephemeralVolumes[*].ebs.encrypted` for EBS-backed ephemeral volumes each turn on Amazon EBS encryption. Enabling it at creation helps protect the data your agents store on these volumes.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider should be placed only in private subnets

mitigationContext.context: The required `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.vpcConfiguration.subnets[*]` request parameter on `CreateCapacityProvider` sets the subnets where AgentCore launches your capacity provider's Amazon EC2 managed instances and their network interfaces. Private subnet placement helps prevent direct internet routing to these instances, reducing their network exposure.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider should use an EC2 instance type that supports automatic encryption of instance-to-instance traffic

mitigationContext.context: AgentCore uses your capacity provider to launch the Amazon EC2 managed instances that run your agent runtime sessions in your VPC. The instance type that AgentCore chooses from your allowed instance types determines whether traffic that your agent code exchanges with other instances you operate can be automatically encrypted in transit, which applies between supported instance types in the same Region on a direct network path.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider's root volume, ephemeral EBS volume, and persistent volume should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: Your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider can specify an AWS KMS customer managed key to encrypt its root volume, ephemeral EBS volume, and persistent volume. Using a customer managed key gives you control over the key's lifecycle and permissions.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider should launch its instances in subnets in more than one Availability Zone.

mitigationContext.context: AgentCore launches your capacity provider's instances and their network interfaces in the subnets that you specify in the `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.vpcConfiguration.subnets[*]` subnet list. Placing those network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone provides network-level redundancy and helps keep connectivity available when one zone is disrupted.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag a capacity provider by passing the `$.tags{key}` key-to-value map to `CreateCapacityProvider`, or later through `TagResource`. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each capacity provider supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider should have detailed monitoring enabled to collect detailed CloudWatch metrics

mitigationContext.context: Detailed monitoring, turned on by setting the `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.launchTemplateSource.launchParameters.monitoring` request parameter to `DETAILED`, sends metrics for your capacity provider's Amazon EC2 managed instances to CloudWatch in 1-minute periods instead of the default 5-minute periods. Collecting those metrics improves security visibility by providing finer-grained data for anomaly detection and incident response.

If another monitoring platform already collects equivalent detailed metrics for this resource, that platform can provide the same visibility for anomaly detection and incident response. Enable this feature when no equivalent collection is in place.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

mitigationContext.context: The `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.vpcConfiguration.securityGroups[*]` request parameter specifies the security groups that govern traffic on the network interfaces of your capacity provider's Amazon EC2 managed instances. Restricting the inbound and outbound rules to the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports helps reduce the network exposure of your capacity provider.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter's execution role should be restricted to accessing resources only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: The `$.executionRoleArn` request parameter designates your code interpreter's execution role, whose credentials the code and commands in its sessions use for AWS API calls. Restricting those calls to expected networks enforces the network perimeter on your identities and helps prevent the use of those credentials from unexpected networks.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter's execution role should be assumed only by Amazon Bedrock AgentCore acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: You can pass an IAM execution role to your code interpreter through the `$.executionRoleArn` request parameter, and the role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter should be in an Amazon VPC

mitigationContext.context: Setting the `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode` network mode to `VPC` places your code interpreter's elastic network interfaces in your VPC subnets, with the security groups you specify. Placing a code interpreter in a VPC is optional and enables network-level isolation and access controls.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter should have elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in more than one Availability Zone (AZ)

mitigationContext.context: AgentCore creates elastic network interfaces for your code interpreter's VPC configuration in the subnets listed in `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.subnets[*]`, the subnet IDs you set at creation. Placing those network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone provides network-level redundancy and helps keep connectivity available when one zone is disrupted.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You can tag a custom code interpreter through the `$.tags{key}` request parameter, a key-to-value map, when you call `CreateCodeInterpreter`, or later by calling `TagResource`. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each code interpreter supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

mitigationContext.context: In VPC mode, the security groups in the `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.securityGroups[*]` request parameter govern traffic on the elastic network interfaces that AgentCore creates in your subnets. Restricting the inbound and outbound rules to the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports helps reduce the network exposure of your code interpreter.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter should be configured to send application logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery

mitigationContext.context: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore produces application logs for `InvokeCodeInterpreter` calls in your code interpreter sessions, recording the code, commands, or file operations and their results. Sending those logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery provides security-relevant visibility.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore configuration bundle's component configuration should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: Your configuration bundle's component configurations, such as system prompts and tool descriptions, can be encrypted with a customer managed key through the `$.kmsKeyArn` request parameter. Configuration bundle metadata, such as the name, description, version IDs, and timestamps, stays encrypted with an AWS owned key. Using a customer managed key gives you control over the key's lifecycle and permissions.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore configuration bundle should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag a configuration bundle through the `$.tags{key}` request parameter, a key-to-value map, when you call `CreateConfigurationBundle`, or on an existing bundle through `TagResource`. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each configuration bundle supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore consent portal's execution role should be assumed only by AgentCore acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Your consent portal binds an IAM execution role through the `$.executionRoleArn` request parameter, and that role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only AgentCore, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore consent portal that uses OIDC to authenticate principals should be configured only with trusted OIDC identity providers

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore consent portal authenticates your end users to the portal through the OIDC identity provider configured in the OAuth2 credential provider that `$.idpConfig.credentialProviderArn` names. Configuring only trusted OIDC identity providers helps prevent an untrusted identity provider from being used to gain unintended access.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore consent portal should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag a consent portal at creation by using the `$.tags{key}` request parameter of `CreateConsentPortal`, a key-to-value map of up to 50 tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each consent portal supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore dataset should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: The `$.kmsKeyArn` request parameter lets you configure your dataset to use a customer managed key for encryption. Using a customer managed key gives you control over the key's lifecycle and permissions.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore dataset should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag a dataset at creation through the `$.tags{key}` request parameter, a key-to-value map that `CreateDataset` accepts, or later through `TagResource`. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each dataset supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore evaluator's instructions and rating scale should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: Your custom evaluator's instructions and rating scale can be envelope-encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key specified in the `$.kmsKeyArn` request parameter. Using a customer managed key helps you control the key's lifecycle and permissions.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore evaluator should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag a custom evaluator at creation through the `$.tags{key}` key-to-value map on `CreateEvaluator`, or later by calling `TagResource`. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each evaluator supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway's service role should be assumed only by AgentCore acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Your gateway's IAM service role, passed in the `$.roleArn` request parameter, has a trust policy that specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only AgentCore, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway should be accessed only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: Requests to your gateway can originate from the internet through its public endpoint or from a VPC through an interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink), and your gateway's resource-based policy can authorize them. A network perimeter helps you confirm that your gateway can be accessed only from expected networks.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway resources

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy on a gateway in another account can grant your principals access to that gateway, subject to their own identity-based policies. The resource perimeter helps restrict your identities to resources your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: When you call `CreateGateway` or `UpdateGateway`, the `$.kmsKeyArn` request parameter sets a customer managed AWS KMS key that encrypts your gateway's data at rest. Unlike the default AWS owned key, a customer managed key gives you control over its lifecycle and lets you audit its use. You can also make your gateway's encrypted data unavailable by disabling the key or revoking the gateway's access to it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway should use AWS IAM for inbound authorization

mitigationContext.context: Your gateway can authenticate callers of its gateway URL by validating JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) from your OAuth identity provider, or accept unauthenticated requests. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore also supports IAM-based inbound authorization for callers of your gateway URL.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway's identity provider private endpoint should have elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in more than one Availability Zone (AZ)

mitigationContext.context: For your gateway's identity provider private endpoint, AgentCore creates a managed VPC Lattice resource gateway with one network interface in each subnet of the `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` subnet list. Placing those network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone provides network-level redundancy and helps keep connectivity available when one zone is disrupted.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway's resource policy should limit permissions to a subset of IAM principals, rather than granting access to all IAM principals

mitigationContext.context: A gateway can carry its own resource-based policy that names the IAM principals allowed to invoke the gateway, set through `$.policy`. Requiring explicit principal definitions rather than wildcard principals helps prevent the gateway from inadvertently being made public or accessible to unintended actors. This mitigation applies to a gateway whose callers authenticate as IAM principals (SigV4). A gateway configured with OAuth (JWT) inbound authorization must name a wildcard principal instead, so this mitigation does not apply to it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway should not allow unauthenticated access to its invocation endpoint

mitigationContext.context: Calls to the invocation endpoint of your gateway can succeed without authentication when its `$.authorizerType` inbound authorization setting is `NONE`. Requiring authentication on that path helps prevent direct unauthenticated access to your gateway.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway should only be configured with a trusted identity provider

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway sets its identity provider through `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl`, which can name identity providers outside AWS. Restricting the identity provider helps keep the JWT bearer tokens your gateway accepts flowing only from trusted targets.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway supports a resource-based policy that specifies who can access it and what actions they can perform. The identity perimeter helps restrict access to your gateways to trusted identities and AWS services acting on your behalf.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway should be accessed by an AWS service principal only when the service principal is acting on behalf of a trusted resource, AWS account, or organization

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy on your gateway can grant an AWS service principal the `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway` action. That policy should restrict which accounts or resources the service may act on behalf of.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway that uses OIDC to authenticate principals should be configured only with trusted OAuth 2.0 authorization servers or OIDC identity providers

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway with JWT-based inbound authorization authenticates callers of its gateway URL through the OAuth 2.0 authorization server or OIDC identity provider whose discovery URL you set in the `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl` request parameter. Configuring only trusted OAuth 2.0 authorization servers or OIDC identity providers helps prevent an untrusted identity provider from being used to gain unintended access.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You can tag a gateway at creation through the `CreateGateway` request parameter `$.tags{key}`, a key-to-value map of tags, or later through `TagResource`. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each gateway supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway's identity provider private endpoint should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

mitigationContext.context: When your gateway's custom JWT authorizer reaches a private identity provider, you can specify security groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` to govern traffic through the AgentCore-managed VPC Lattice resource gateway's network interfaces in your subnets, with your VPC's default security group applying when you specify none. Restricting the inbound and outbound rules to the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports helps reduce the network exposure of your gateway's identity provider private endpoint.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway should be configured to send application logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery

mitigationContext.context: As your gateway processes MCP requests, its application logs record authorization header errors, invalid tool or method parameters, target configuration errors, and request and response bodies. Sending those logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery provides security-relevant visibility.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway target's private endpoint should be placed only in private subnets

mitigationContext.context: For a managed private endpoint, the required `$.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` request parameter sets the subnets that hold its VPC Lattice resource gateway network interfaces. Private subnet placement helps prevent direct internet routing to your gateway target's private endpoint, reducing its network exposure.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway target should be in an Amazon VPC

mitigationContext.context: With a private endpoint, a gateway target reaches its backend through a VPC Lattice resource gateway whose network interfaces sit in your VPC subnets. Placing a gateway target in a VPC is optional and enables network-level isolation and access controls.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway target's private endpoint should have elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in more than one Availability Zone (AZ)

mitigationContext.context: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore places the network interfaces of your gateway target's managed private endpoint in each subnet of the `$.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` subnet list. Placing those network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone provides network-level redundancy and helps keep connectivity available when one zone is disrupted.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway target should only be configured with a trusted HTTP endpoint

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway target sets its endpoint through `$.targetConfiguration.mcp.mcpServer.endpoint`, `$.targetConfiguration.http.passthrough.endpoint`, `$.targetConfiguration.inference.provider.endpoint` or the Smithy model's endpoint rule set from `$.targetConfiguration.mcp.smithyModel.inlinePayload` or `$.targetConfiguration.mcp.smithyModel.s3.uri`, which can name HTTP endpoints outside AWS. Restricting the endpoint helps keep tool calls, model requests and outbound credentials flowing only to trusted targets.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway target's managed VPC Lattice resource gateway should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

mitigationContext.context: For a managed private endpoint, you can associate your own security groups with the managed VPC Lattice resource gateway's network interfaces through `$.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` instead of the VPC's default security group. Restricting the inbound and outbound rules to the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports helps reduce the network exposure of the managed VPC Lattice resource gateway.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness's execution role should be restricted to accessing resources only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: The `$.executionRoleArn` request parameter designates your harness's IAM execution role, and code in each session's microVM calls AWS services with that role's credentials. Restricting those calls to expected networks enforces the network perimeter on your identities and helps prevent the use of those credentials from unexpected networks.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness's execution role should be assumed only by Amazon Bedrock AgentCore acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: You set your harness's IAM execution role through the `$.executionRoleArn` request parameter, and the role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness should be in an Amazon VPC

mitigationContext.context: Setting your harness to VPC mode places elastic network interfaces for its managed AgentCore Runtime in the subnets you specify, with your security groups attached. Placing a harness in a VPC is optional and enables network-level isolation and access controls.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness's managed memory should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: Your harness's managed memory stores conversation events and long-term memory records, encrypted at rest with an AWS owned key by default. The `$.memory.managedMemoryConfiguration.encryptionKeyArn` request parameter of `CreateHarness` sets a customer managed key for that memory, and the memory's key can't be changed after creation. With a customer managed key, you control the key lifecycle and can audit its use or disable it to make the stored data unavailable.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness should have elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in more than one Availability Zone (AZ)

mitigationContext.context: In VPC network mode, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore creates network interfaces for your harness in the subnets listed in the `$.environment.agentCoreRuntimeEnvironment.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.subnets[*]` VPC subnet setting. Placing those network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone provides network-level redundancy and helps keep connectivity available when one zone is disrupted.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness that uses an inbound JWT authorizer to authenticate principals should be configured only with trusted OAuth 2.0 authorization servers or OIDC identity providers
