implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends a trust policy that restricts assumption of your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime's execution role, `$.roleArn`, to the `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com` service principal with the `aws:SourceArn` and `aws:SourceAccount` condition keys. These conditions help prevent AgentCore from assuming the role on behalf of agent runtimes outside the sources you specify.

Confirm that IAM role trust policies grant access only to the AWS service principals you intend. Review the `Principal` element of each policy and verify it names only the service principals your workload requires.

As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation guidance recommends restricting `sts:AssumeRole` with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key in a resource control policy (RCP), while exempting AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) and scoping those service requests with `aws:SourceOrgID`. These conditions help prevent principals outside your organization from assuming your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime's execution role, `$.roleArn`.

To restrict access to trusted identities, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys to restrict service access to your roles. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation guidance recommends governing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls against your agent runtime with the `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:SourceVpc`, and `aws:RequestedRegion` condition keys in its resource-based policy. These conditions help restrict those calls to expected networks, while exempting AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:ViaAWSService`) and tagged principals (`aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude:network`).

To restrict access to expected networks, use the `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:SourceVpce` condition keys. These scope access to a specific VPC or VPC endpoint. Because VPC IDs are unique only within a Region, pair `aws:SourceVpc` with `aws:RequestedRegion`. Use `aws:SourceIp` with your public IP ranges for requests that do not traverse a VPC endpoint. Use `aws:ViaAWSService` to exempt AWS services that call with your credentials through forward access sessions (FAS). Use `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` to exempt AWS services that access your resources with their service principals. Use `aws:PrincipalTag/tag-key` to exempt principals that must legitimately operate from outside your expected networks. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation guidance recommends validating the resource-based policy declared in `$.Policy` for your agent runtime with a public-access check before provisioning the policy resource. A policy that can grant public access fails this check, helping prevent a public-access grant on your agent runtime from being provisioned.

This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.Policy`, your agent runtime's resource-based policy, for network condition keys such as `aws:SourceVpc` and `aws:VpceOrgID` before provisioning the policy resource. That check helps prevent a resource-based policy that does not restrict access to expected networks from being provisioned on your agent runtime.

This implementation guidance recommends applying the `aws:ResourceOrgID` condition key in a service control policy (SCP) to govern Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls. As a result, your identities are restricted from invoking or managing agent runtimes outside your organization, except through OAuth inbound authentication, which uses JWTs instead of IAM credentials.

To restrict access to trusted resources, use the `aws:ResourceOrgID`, `aws:ResourceOrgPaths`, or `aws:ResourceAccount` condition keys. These scope access to resources that belong to a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.NetworkConfiguration.NetworkMode` set to `VPC`, the network mode of your agent runtime, or `$.CapacityProviderConfiguration.CapacityProviderArn`, the capacity provider that defines your runtime's VPC networking, before provisioning. That check helps prevent an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime from being provisioned without that VPC configuration, so its network traffic can traverse your VPC subnets under your security groups.

A CloudFormation Hook can help verify that your developers specify the `VPC` value for `$.NetworkConfiguration.NetworkMode`, rather than `PUBLIC`. Agent runtimes that declare `$.CapacityProviderConfiguration.CapacityProviderArn` pass the check because they inherit VPC networking from their capacity provider. In `VPC` mode, the runtime's network interfaces receive private IP addresses from your subnets. This placement supports the network perimeter objective that your identities can access resources only from expected networks.

This implementation guidance recommends monitoring AWS CloudTrail management events for the `CreateAgentRuntime` and `UpdateAgentRuntime` calls that create and update your agent runtimes. Flagging requests that set `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode`, the runtime's network mode, to a value other than `VPC` helps you detect runtimes that run outside your VPC. Because the default network mode is `PUBLIC`, also flag `CreateAgentRuntime` requests omitting both `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode` and `$.capacityProviderConfiguration.capacityProviderArn`, the capacity provider that defines the runtime's networking.

Consider monitoring `CreateAgentRuntime`, `UpdateAgentRuntime`, `CreateBrowser`, and `CreateCodeInterpreter` calls in CloudTrail management events. Review `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode`, the request parameter that sets each resource's network mode. Each event also records the calling identity in its `userIdentity` field. If a call places a resource outside your VPC, remediate it with the responsive controls of your choice.

This implementation guidance recommends flagging agent runtimes whose `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode`, their network mode, is absent or not `VPC`. Surfacing them helps you detect agents that run without your VPC's network isolation.

This implementation guidance recommends applying the `bedrock-agentcore:subnets` condition key in a service control policy (SCP) to govern `bedrock-agentcore:CreateAgentRuntime` and `bedrock-agentcore:UpdateAgentRuntime`. This condition helps prevent principals in your organization from deploying Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtimes without a VPC attachment. Requests for Instances runtimes carry no such key, so the condition also restricts them unless the principal carries the policy's exemption tag.

This guidance follows the data perimeter recommendation to use `bedrock-agentcore:subnets` to restrict agent runtime deployment to a customer managed VPC. Running agent runtimes in your VPC lets you inspect their outbound requests by using VPC endpoint policies. This placement helps you apply your identity and resource perimeter controls and enforce your network perimeter.

guidance.description:
When you connect an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime to your VPC (network mode `VPC`), supply two or more subnets in different Availability Zones. Set them in `$.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.subnets[*]` when you call `CreateAgentRuntime` or `UpdateAgentRuntime`, or in the `NetworkConfiguration` property of `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Runtime` in AWS CloudFormation. AgentCore creates elastic network interfaces (ENIs) for the runtime in the subnets you specify. Subnets in different zones place those ENIs in more than one Availability Zone. This helps the runtime's network connectivity survive the loss of a single zone. For runtimes on the Instances compute type, the capacity provider supplies the networking. Apply the same multi-AZ subnet selection to the subnets in the capacity provider's VPC configuration.

Availability Zone membership is a property of each subnet, not of the agent runtime. Before you supply subnet IDs, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation. Confirm from the `AvailabilityZone` and `AvailabilityZoneId` response fields that the subnets resolve to distinct Availability Zones. Also confirm that each zone ID is one that AgentCore supports for VPC connectivity in your Region. Subnets in unsupported zones cause the configuration to fail during resource creation. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so that the templates and modules that create agent runtimes consistently supply at least two subnets from different Availability Zones.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetAgentRuntime` and read `$.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.subnets[*]` from the response. Then resolve the Availability Zones of those subnets with `DescribeSubnets`. You can also enumerate the ENIs with `DescribeNetworkInterfaces`, filtered by those subnets and the runtime's security groups. If your account hides Amazon EC2 managed resources, set `IncludeManagedResources` to `true` so that the results include ENIs that AWS services manage. Confirm that those ENIs are in more than one Availability Zone. AgentCore shares these ENIs among runtimes that use the same subnet and security group configuration. A network settings change creates a new runtime version, and only the `DEFAULT` endpoint moves to it automatically. Call `UpdateAgentRuntimeEndpoint` for custom endpoints that pin earlier versions so that requests to them resolve to the multi-AZ configuration.

If your runtime mounts Amazon EFS or Amazon S3 Files access points, create a mount target in every Availability Zone that your runtime subnets use. An agent placed in a zone without a mount target can fail to mount the file system.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, you can use AWS Resilience Hub. Add the resources of the application that uses your agent runtime to a Resilience Hub application, and run a resiliency assessment. The assessment can flag single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. Before you rely on it for your agent runtime, confirm that Resilience Hub supports the runtime's resource type.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.subnets[*]`, the subnets in your agent runtime's VPC network configuration. Spreading the elastic network interfaces that Amazon Bedrock AgentCore creates for your agent runtime across zones helps the runtime's VPC connectivity survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

This implementation guidance recommends validating, before provisioning, that `$.NetworkConfiguration.NetworkModeConfig.Subnets[*]`, your agent runtime's VPC subnets, lists two or more subnet entries. That check helps prevent a single-subnet agent runtime from being provisioned, so your agent runtime's network interfaces can span more than one Availability Zone.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.subnets[*]`, the subnets where AgentCore creates elastic network interfaces for your agent runtime, then resolving each subnet's Availability Zone. Flagging a VPC-connected microVM agent runtime confined to a single Availability Zone helps you detect agent runtime network interfaces that lack multi-zone redundancy.

This implementation guidance recommends governing invocation and session actions in your agent runtime's resource-based policy, `$.policy`, with the `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition key. As a result, principals outside the accounts you name are restricted from invoking your runtime and its sessions, even when they know its ARN. This guidance applies to an agent runtime whose callers authenticate as IAM principals (SigV4). An agent runtime configured with OAuth authentication must name a wildcard principal instead, so this guidance does not apply to it.

Confirm that resource-based policies grant access only to authorized identities. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys to restrict access to trusted identities. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation guidance recommends evaluating the resource-based policy at `$.policy` on each listed agent runtime for grants to a wildcard principal. Flagging an agent runtime whose policy grants access to a wildcard principal without an organization condition helps you detect a policy that can grant public access.

This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.AuthorizerConfiguration.CustomJWTAuthorizer.DiscoveryUrl`, the inbound JWT authorizer's discovery URL, before provisioning. That check helps prevent an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime from being provisioned with an OpenID Connect discovery URL outside your organization's trust boundary.

A CloudFormation Hook can help prevent developers from specifying an authorizer configuration that does not belong to your organization on `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Runtime` resources. The check applies to `$.AuthorizerConfiguration.CustomJWTAuthorizer.DiscoveryUrl`, which points to the identity provider whose tokens your agent runtime validates.

This implementation guidance recommends recording `CreateAgentRuntime` and `UpdateAgentRuntime` calls together with `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl`, the OpenID Connect discovery URL of your agent runtime's inbound JWT authorizer. Recording those calls helps you detect an agent runtime configured with an OpenID Connect identity provider discovery URL outside your organization, from which it accepts bearer tokens.

Monitoring `CreateAgentRuntime` and `UpdateAgentRuntime` management events for their inbound authorizer configuration helps you detect an agent runtime that trusts an identity provider outside your organization. Each event records `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl` in its request parameters and the calling identity in its `userIdentity` field. Compare the full recorded URL, host and path, with the discovery URLs you trust. A provider such as Amazon Cognito serves every user pool from one regional host (`cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com`). It identifies each pool only by the user pool ID segment of the path. If necessary, remediate with the responsive controls of your choice.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl`, the OpenID Connect discovery URL of the inbound JWT authorizer, recorded on each agent runtime version. Flagging a JWT authorizer discovery URL you have not designated as trusted helps you detect acceptance of bearer tokens issued outside your trust boundary.

This implementation guidance recommends governing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls against your agent runtime with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key in its resource-based policy, while exempting AWS services that access it on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) and scoping those service requests with `aws:SourceOrgID`. These conditions help prevent identities outside your organization from accessing your agent runtime.

Confirm that resource-based policies grant access only to trusted identities and to services acting on your behalf. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys to restrict access to trusted identities. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. To restrict service access to your resources, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.Policy`, the resource-based policy document for your agent runtime, before provisioning the resource-based policy on that runtime. The hook helps prevent a policy that can grant access beyond your reference policy, permissions you specify, or access to an AWS service principal beyond a reference policy containing the source conditions you accept from being provisioned.

This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoNewAccess`, `CheckAccessNotGranted`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain or grant specified permissions. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals that may be granted access to the resource. The check fails when the resource-based policy grants access beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for resource-based policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept on grants to an AWS service principal: one statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the policy grants a service principal access that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

Flagging those grants helps you detect invocation and session access to your agent runtime that extends beyond trusted identities.

Custom policy checks (`CheckNoNewAccess`, `CheckAccessNotGranted`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain or grant specified permissions. implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.AuthorizerConfiguration.CustomJWTAuthorizer.DiscoveryUrl`, the OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider that your agent runtime's inbound JWT authorizer trusts to authenticate callers, before provisioning. Requiring trusted OIDC identity providers helps prevent an agent runtime that designates an untrusted provider from being provisioned.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl`, the OpenID Connect discovery URL of the identity provider whose JWT bearer tokens authenticate callers to your agent runtime. Flagging an agent runtime whose recorded provider you do not trust helps you detect an authentication path that could allow unintended access.

This implementation guidance recommends validating, before provisioning, that `$.Tags{key}` declares owner and purpose tags. Requiring those tags helps prevent an agent runtime that omits them from being provisioned and helps keep ownership and business function attributable.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.tags{key}` on each Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime listed through `$.agentRuntimes[*].agentRuntimeArn` and flagging any that omit your required owner and purpose tag keys. Surfacing those resources helps you attribute each Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime to an accountable owner and the business function it supports.

This implementation guidance recommends restricting `bedrock-agentcore:CreateAgentRuntime` and `bedrock-agentcore:TagResource` with the `aws:RequestTag/owner`, `aws:RequestTag/purpose`, and `aws:TagKeys` condition keys in a service control policy (SCP). These conditions help prevent creating or tagging an agent runtime without the owner and purpose tag keys, or removing them through `bedrock-agentcore:UntagResource`.

Use `aws:RequestTag/owner` and `aws:RequestTag/purpose` so that a request omitting either one is denied. Use `aws:TagKeys` to require each key in its exact case because the tag-key portion of `aws:RequestTag/tag-key` is not case-sensitive. Also use `aws:TagKeys` on the untag action so that a request removing either key is denied.

guidance.description:
Configure the security groups associated with your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime following least-privilege best practices. In VPC network mode, the security groups in `$.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.securityGroups[*]` are attached to the elastic network interfaces (ENIs) that AgentCore creates in your subnets. These security groups control which resources your agent code can communicate with. Your runtime's custom JWT authorizer may reach a private identity provider through a managed VPC Lattice resource gateway. In that case, the security groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` govern that gateway's traffic. Specify those security groups explicitly, because the VPC's default security group is used when none are given.

Restrict both inbound and outbound rules on these security groups to only the required sources and destinations, protocols, and ports. Sources and destinations can be IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists. Avoid rules that permit unrestricted access from or to any IP address (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0), particularly on administrative or sensitive ports. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. For example, reference the security group of a database or file system mount target that your agent code connects to. For example, the scope can match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. guidance.description:
This guidance applies to custom browsers that you create in the `VPC` network mode. When you call `CreateBrowser`, configure `networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.subnets` with two or more private subnets in different Availability Zones. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore creates elastic network interfaces (ENIs) for the browser in the subnets you specify. The Availability Zones of those subnets determine where the browser's ENIs exist. Spreading the ENIs across zones helps the browser keep network connectivity if a single Availability Zone becomes unavailable. Because a browser has no update operation, its subnet list is fixed at creation. To change the subnets, delete the browser and create it again.

Subnet-to-AZ membership is a property of each subnet, not of the browser. Before you supply subnet IDs, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation and confirm that the `AvailabilityZone` values differ. Also confirm that each subnet's `AvailabilityZoneId` is a zone that AgentCore supports for VPC connectivity in your Region. Subnets in unsupported zones cause browser creation to fail. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review for the templates and modules that create your browsers. Confirm that each one supplies at least two subnets from different Availability Zones, for example in the `Subnets` property of `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::BrowserCustom`.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetBrowser` and read the subnet IDs returned in `networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.subnets`. Then call `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` with a `subnet-id` filter for those subnets. AgentCore tags the ENIs it manages with the `AmazonBedrockAgentCoreManaged` tag. Confirm that the returned ENIs span more than one Availability Zone. These ENIs can be shared with other AgentCore resources that use the same subnet and security group configuration.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, include the application resources around your browsers in an AWS Resilience Hub application. Then run a resiliency assessment against your resiliency policy. The assessment can flag resources concentrated in a single Availability Zone. The AWS Resilience Hub list of supported resources does not name Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Confirm which of your resources the assessment covers before you rely on it for your browsers.

guidance.description:
For an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore custom browser in VPC network mode, configure the security groups in `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.securityGroups[*]` of your `CreateBrowser` request following least-privilege best practices. AgentCore attaches these groups to the elastic network interfaces that it creates in your subnets. Their inbound and outbound rules control which resources your browser sessions can communicate with. The association is set when you create the browser. You maintain least privilege through the rules on the referenced security groups. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. Avoid rules that permit unrestricted access from or to any address (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0), particularly on administrative or sensitive ports. If your browser sessions need internet access through a NAT gateway, limit those outbound rules to the protocols and ports that your browsing workload requires. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope these policies by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or a block list. It flags noncompliant security groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can automatically remediate them. A usage audit security group policy removes unused or redundant security groups. A content audit policy can evaluate the groups your browser references, because they are customer-created security groups. Before you rely on a common security group policy for your browser, confirm that Firewall Manager supports the network interfaces that AgentCore manages.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access that you consider unintended. For example, match any path that reaches your browser's network interfaces on administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. Create the scope with `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, run an analysis with `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer evaluates the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

guidance.description:
Create each Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider with two or more subnets that reside in different Availability Zones (AZs). Supply these subnets in the VPC configuration of your `CreateCapacityProvider` request, at `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.vpcConfiguration.subnets[*]`. AgentCore launches the capacity provider's Amazon EC2 managed instances and their elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in these subnets. Agent runtimes on the Instances compute type inherit this networking. With subnets in more than one zone, the ENIs for your agent sessions can exist in more than one Availability Zone. This helps network connectivity survive the loss of a single zone.

Plan the subnet list before you create the capacity provider. The service accepts a single subnet. You also can't change the subnet list later, because `UpdateCapacityProvider` changes only the description. In AWS CloudFormation, changing the subnets of an `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::CapacityProvider` resource requires replacement. To move a single-zone capacity provider to multiple zones, create a new one, for example through the console's duplicate flow. Then associate your agent runtimes with the new capacity provider. Deleting the original capacity provider stops and deletes its sessions and their persistent storage. Copy out any session data you need before you delete it.

Subnet-to-AZ membership is a property of each subnet, not of the capacity provider. Before you supply subnet IDs, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation. Confirm from each subnet's `AvailabilityZone` field that the IDs belong to distinct Availability Zones. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so that every template and module that creates a capacity provider supplies subnets from at least two Availability Zones.

To verify the deployed configuration, call `GetCapacityProvider`. Confirm that the subnets in the returned VPC configuration resolve to more than one Availability Zone. To inspect running sessions, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeInstances` operation with managed resources included. Filter on the `bedrock-agentcore:capacity-provider-id` tag key. You can also call `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` with `IncludeManagedResources` set to `true`. Confirm that the subnets of the attached network interfaces span more than one Availability Zone. Depending on your managed resource visibility setting, EC2 list operations can hide these resources unless you include managed resources. Instances exist only while sessions run. Treat the configured subnet list as the primary check.

Some constraints remain zonal. Amazon EBS volumes attach only to instances in the same Availability Zone. A session that resumes with persistent volumes may therefore depend on the zone where those volumes were created. Capacity Reservations also reserve capacity in a specific Availability Zone. If you use the `capacity-reservations-only` preference, target reservations in more than one of your subnets' Availability Zones.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, include your application's resources in an AWS Resilience Hub application. Then run a resiliency assessment to flag single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. AWS Resilience Hub does not list Amazon Bedrock AgentCore among its supported services. It may therefore report the capacity provider as unsupported. Use the assessment to complement the configuration checks above, not to replace them.

guidance.description:
Configure the security groups that you specify for your capacity provider in `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.vpcConfiguration.securityGroups[*]` on `CreateCapacityProvider` by following least-privilege best practices. AgentCore associates these groups with the Amazon EC2 managed instances that it launches in your VPC. Agent runtimes that use the capacity provider inherit this networking. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. Do not permit unrestricted access from or to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, particularly on administrative ports such as port 22 (SSH). A new security group includes an outbound rule that allows all outbound traffic. Replace that rule with rules for the specific destinations your agents require, and do not open broad outbound access unless your agents need it. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, such as a database or an interface VPC endpoint that your agents connect to, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change. After you create a capacity provider, you can't change which security groups it uses, because `UpdateCapacityProvider` changes only the description. To use different groups, create a new capacity provider, for example through the console's duplicate flow. You can still tighten the rules in the referenced groups at any time. Rule changes apply automatically to all resources associated with each group.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations, scoped by account, OU, or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline group to in-scope resources. Because you can't directly modify instances that AgentCore manages, a common policy may not be able to change their security group associations. A content audit policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or block list. It flags noncompliant groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can automatically remediate. Include the Amazon VPC security group resource type in its scope so that the groups your capacity provider references are evaluated directly. Review the findings before you enable automatic remediation. A usage audit policy removes unused or redundant groups, and it can treat a group as unused when no EC2 instance or network interface uses it. AgentCore launches instances when your runtimes are invoked, so your capacity provider's groups can have no attached network interfaces between sessions. Review usage audit findings before you enable automatic removal. Deleting a group that your capacity provider references may prevent AgentCore from launching new instances.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended, such as any path that reaches port 22 on your capacity provider's instances from an unrestricted address. Then run an analysis (`CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`) and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer reasons about the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. It identifies unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements. Run analyses while your capacity provider has active sessions, because its instances and their network interfaces exist only for the duration of a session.

In VPC mode, session traffic can traverse your VPC, where your network perimeter controls can apply. The same recommendation applies to agent runtimes and custom browsers.

This implementation guidance recommends monitoring CloudTrail management events for `CreateCodeInterpreter` calls, focusing on `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode`, the network mode of the new code interpreter. The `CreateCodeInterpreter`, `CreateBrowser`, `CreateAgentRuntime`, and `UpdateAgentRuntime` calls each carry `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode`, the network mode of the resource they configure. Monitoring these calls helps you detect resources configured with a network mode other than `VPC`. If necessary, remediate with the responsive controls of your choice, such as recreating a code interpreter in VPC mode.

This implementation guidance recommends flagging Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreters whose `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode`, the network mode, is not `VPC`. Surfacing them helps you detect code interpreter sessions that run without network interfaces in your VPC subnets.

This implementation guidance recommends applying the `bedrock-agentcore:subnets` condition key in a service control policy (SCP) to govern `bedrock-agentcore:CreateCodeInterpreter`. This condition helps prevent principals in your organization from deploying Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreters without a VPC attachment.

Restricting non-VPC deployment is a data-perimeter control for services that support optional VPC placement. Applying the `bedrock-agentcore:subnets` condition key to `bedrock-agentcore:CreateCodeInterpreter` in a service control policy (SCP) helps restrict code interpreter creation to VPCs that you manage. A VPC placement lets you apply identity and resource perimeter controls in VPC endpoint policies and enforce your network perimeter.

guidance.description:
This guidance applies to custom code interpreters that set `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode` to `VPC`. When you call `CreateCodeInterpreter`, list two or more subnets in different Availability Zones (AZs) in `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.subnets[*]`. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore creates elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in those subnets through the `AWSServiceRoleForBedrockAgentCoreNetwork` service-linked role. Subnets in different AZs let AgentCore place your code interpreter's ENIs in more than one AZ. This helps your code interpreter's VPC connectivity survive the loss of a single AZ. If your code interpreter mounts Amazon EFS or Amazon S3 Files access points, create a mount target in each AZ that your subnets use.

Each subnet belongs to one AZ, so the code interpreter's AZ coverage depends on the subnets you choose. Before you supply subnet IDs, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation and confirm that their `AvailabilityZone` values differ. Also check each `AvailabilityZoneId` against the AZs that AgentCore supports for VPC connectivity in your Region. Subnets in unsupported AZs cause code interpreter creation to fail. Code interpreters have no update operation, so the subnet list is fixed at creation. In AWS CloudFormation, changing the `Subnets` property of `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::CodeInterpreterCustom` requires replacing the resource. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review of the templates and modules that create code interpreters. Confirm that each one supplies at least two subnets from different AZs. To correct an existing code interpreter, create a replacement with a corrected subnet list. Stop the original's active sessions before you delete it.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetCodeInterpreter` and note the subnets in `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.subnets[*]` and the security groups it returns. Then call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` operation, filtering by those subnet and security group IDs. If your account's managed resource visibility is hidden, set `IncludeManagedResources` to `true` so the results can include ENIs that AgentCore provisions. Confirm that the returned ENIs span more than one AZ. AgentCore shares ENIs across agents that use the same subnet and security group configuration, so a returned ENI might also serve other resources.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, use AWS Resilience Hub. Include your code interpreter's application resources in a Resilience Hub application and run a resiliency assessment. The assessment can flag single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. The Resilience Hub list of supported services doesn't include Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Confirm what your assessment covers. Keep the subnet and ENI checks as your direct verification for the code interpreter.

This implementation guidance recommends validating, before provisioning, that `$.NetworkConfiguration.VpcConfig.Subnets[*]`, your code interpreter's VPC subnets, lists two or more subnet entries. Use `aws:RequestTag/owner` and `aws:RequestTag/purpose` so that a request omitting either one is denied. guidance.description:
This guidance applies to custom code interpreters that use `VPC` network mode. Configure their security groups following least-privilege best practices. These are the groups you specify in `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.securityGroups[*]` when you call `CreateCodeInterpreter`. AgentCore attaches them to the elastic network interfaces it creates in your subnets. Their rules help control which VPC resources, AWS service endpoints, and NAT-routed internet destinations your code interpreter sessions can communicate with.

Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. Avoid rules that allow unrestricted access from or to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, particularly on administrative or sensitive ports. A new security group includes an outbound rule that allows all outbound traffic. Replace that rule with outbound rules for only the destinations your sessions need. When the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. Examples of such peers include a database or a file system mount target in your VPC. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change.

You can't change which security groups a code interpreter uses after you create it. Define least-privilege groups before you call `CreateCodeInterpreter`. You can still tighten the rules in those groups later. Rule changes apply automatically to all resources associated with the group. To use different groups, recreate the code interpreter.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope these policies by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or a block list. It flags noncompliant groups in a central dashboard, notifies you, and can automatically remediate noncompliant rules. A usage audit security group policy removes unused or redundant security groups. Include the Amazon VPC security group resource type in your content audit policy scope. This brings the groups your code interpreter uses into scope, even though AgentCore creates and manages the network interfaces they attach to. Before you rely on a common policy, confirm that it can apply to the network interfaces that AgentCore manages.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended. For example, match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. You can also match outbound paths from your code interpreter's network interfaces to an internet gateway when you don't intend internet access. Create the scope by calling `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`. Run an analysis by calling `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and then review the findings. Network Access Analyzer evaluates your security groups together with route tables, network ACLs, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security requirements.

This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one sts:AssumeRole statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

Flagging Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateways whose key is not a customer managed key in your account, or whose key material is imported or held in an external key store, helps you detect where you do not control the key policy, lifecycle, or key material.

This implementation guidance recommends applying the `bedrock-agentcore:KmsKeyArn` condition key in a service control policy (SCP) to govern `bedrock-agentcore:CreateGateway` and `bedrock-agentcore:UpdateGateway`. This condition helps prevent creating or modifying an AgentCore gateway without an approved customer managed key at `$.kmsKeyArn`, the key that encrypts the gateway's data at rest.

This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.AuthorizerType`, your gateway's inbound authorizer type, for the declared value `NONE` rather than `CUSTOM_JWT`, `AWS_IAM`, or `AUTHENTICATE_ONLY` before provisioning. That validation helps prevent a gateway invocation endpoint that accepts unauthenticated requests from being provisioned.

This implementation guidance recommends validating that `$.AuthorizerType`, the inbound authorizer type for your gateway, is set to `AWS_IAM` for IAM-based inbound authorization before provisioning. This validation helps prevent an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway that relies only on JSON Web Token (JWT)-based or offloaded inbound authorization from being provisioned.

This implementation guidance recommends reading the value recorded at `$.configuration.AuthorizerType`, your gateway's inbound authorizer type. Flagging a value of `NONE` helps you detect gateways whose invocation endpoint can accept unauthenticated requests.

This implementation guidance recommends flagging an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway whose `$.configuration.AuthorizerType`, its inbound authorizer type, is `CUSTOM_JWT`, `AUTHENTICATE_ONLY`, or `NONE` instead of `AWS_IAM`. Flagging these gateways helps you detect where callers can reach your gateway targets without an identity-based or resource-based policy granting them `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway`.

guidance.description:
Your gateway's `CUSTOM_JWT` authorizer can reach a private (VPC-hosted) identity provider through a managed private endpoint. In that configuration, supply two or more subnets from different Availability Zones (AZs) in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` when you call `CreateGateway` or `UpdateGateway`. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore places a managed VPC Lattice resource gateway in these subnets, with an elastic network interface (ENI) in each subnet. AgentCore uses these ENIs to reach your identity provider's OIDC discovery and JWKS endpoints. Spreading the ENIs across zones helps that connectivity survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

Each subnet resides entirely within one Availability Zone. The subnets you choose therefore define the endpoint's zone footprint. Before you supply subnet IDs, call `DescribeSubnets` and confirm from the `AvailabilityZone` field that the subnets belong to distinct Availability Zones. Also confirm that your identity provider's OIDC discovery and JWKS endpoints are reachable from every subnet you supply. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so that templates and modules that create or update the gateway supply at least two such subnets.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetGateway` and review the subnet IDs returned in its authorizer configuration. You can also call `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` with a `subnet-id` filter for those subnets. Confirm that the resource gateway's network interfaces span more than one Availability Zone.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, you can include your gateway's application resources in an AWS Resilience Hub application. Then run a resiliency assessment, which can flag single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. Resilience Hub does not currently list Amazon Bedrock AgentCore or Amazon VPC Lattice among its supported services. Confirm coverage before you rely on its findings for this endpoint.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`, the subnet IDs of your gateway's identity provider managed private endpoint. Spreading the network interfaces of the VPC Lattice resource gateway that AgentCore creates across zones helps connectivity to your private identity provider survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

This implementation guidance recommends validating, before provisioning, that `$.AuthorizerConfiguration.CustomJWTAuthorizer.PrivateEndpoint.ManagedVpcResource.SubnetIds[*]`, your identity provider private endpoint's VPC subnets, lists two or more subnet entries. That check helps prevent a single-subnet identity provider private endpoint from being provisioned, so the endpoint's network interfaces can span more than one Availability Zone.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`, the subnets that host your gateway's identity provider managed private endpoint, then resolving each subnet's Availability Zone. Flagging a gateway with a managed private endpoint confined to a single Availability Zone helps you detect identity provider private endpoint network interfaces that lack multi-zone redundancy.

This implementation guidance recommends governing `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway` in your AgentCore gateway's resource-based policy, `$.policy`, with the `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition key. As a result, principals outside the accounts you name are restricted from invoking your gateway, even when they can reach its invocation URL. This guidance applies to an AgentCore gateway whose callers authenticate as IAM principals (SigV4). An AgentCore gateway configured with OAuth authentication must name a wildcard principal instead, so this guidance does not apply to it.

Confirm that resource-based policies grant access only to authorized identities. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys to restrict access to trusted identities. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation guidance recommends evaluating the resource-based policy of each listed gateway at `$.policy` for grants to a wildcard principal. Flagging a gateway whose policy grants access to a wildcard principal without an organization condition helps you detect a policy that can grant public access.

This implementation guidance recommends applying the `bedrock-agentcore:GatewayAuthorizerType` condition key in a service control policy (SCP) to govern `bedrock-agentcore:CreateGateway` and `bedrock-agentcore:UpdateGateway`. This condition helps prevent principals in your organization from creating or modifying an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway with `NONE`, the No Authorization inbound authorizer type, which allows unauthenticated access to the gateway's invocation endpoint.

This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.AuthorizerConfiguration.CustomJWTAuthorizer.DiscoveryUrl`, the identity provider discovery URL for inbound JWT authorization, before provisioning. That check helps prevent an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway from being provisioned with an identity provider's issuer path outside your organization's trust boundary.

Within your resource perimeter, a CloudFormation Hook can help prevent developers from specifying a gateway authorizer that trusts an identity provider outside your organization. The hook confirms that `$.AuthorizerConfiguration.CustomJWTAuthorizer.DiscoveryUrl` matches the full discovery URL, host and path, of an identity provider you trust before the gateway is provisioned. For example, Amazon Cognito user pools that use the default issuer share one regional host (`cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com`). These pools differ only in the user-pool-ID segment of the path. A host-only comparison would therefore admit every such pool in the Region.

This implementation guidance recommends recording `CreateGateway` and `UpdateGateway` calls together with `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl`, the OpenID Connect discovery URL of the gateway's inbound JWT authorizer. Recording those calls helps you detect a gateway configured with an identity provider discovery URL outside your organization, from which it accepts tokens.

Monitoring `CreateGateway` and `UpdateGateway` calls for `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl` helps you identify gateways whose inbound JWT authorizer trusts an identity provider outside your organization. Each management event also records the identity that made the call. Compare the full recorded URL, host and path, with the discovery URLs you trust. Amazon Cognito user pools that use the default issuer share one regional host (`cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com`); only the user pool ID segment of the path identifies each pool, so a host-only comparison would admit every such pool in the Region. You can then remediate with the responsive controls of your choice.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.configuration.AuthorizerConfiguration`, the custom JWT authorizer whose discovery URL names the OIDC identity provider that authenticates callers to your gateway. Flagging an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway whose recorded provider you do not trust helps you detect an authentication path that could allow unintended access.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.configuration.AuthorizerConfiguration`, the inbound authorizer configuration that carries your identity provider's discovery URL, recorded on each Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway. Flagging an identity provider discovery URL you have not designated as trusted helps you detect acceptance of inbound tokens issued outside your trust boundary.

This implementation guidance recommends restricting `bedrock-agentcore:CreateGateway` and `bedrock-agentcore:UpdateGateway` with the `bedrock-agentcore:DiscoveryUrl` condition key in a service control policy (SCP). This condition helps prevent an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway from being configured with an identity provider discovery URL you have not designated as trusted.

The data perimeter policy examples apply the `bedrock-agentcore:DiscoveryUrl` condition key in a service control policy (SCP) to gateway creation and updates. Your gateway validates inbound JWT bearer tokens by using metadata and public keys fetched from its discovery URL. Restricting that URL helps prevent your gateways from relying on an identity provider you have not designated as trusted.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends governing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls against your gateway with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key in its resource-based policy, while exempting AWS services that access it on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) and scoping those service requests with `aws:SourceOrgID`. These conditions help prevent identities outside your organization from accessing your gateway.

Confirm that resource-based policies grant access only to trusted identities and to services acting on your behalf. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys to restrict access to trusted identities. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. To restrict service access to your resources, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.Policy`, the resource-based policy that controls who can invoke your gateway, before provisioning your AgentCore gateway's resource policy. The hook helps prevent a policy that can grant access beyond your reference policy, permissions you specify such as `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway`, or access to an AWS service principal beyond a reference policy containing the source conditions you accept from being provisioned.

This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoNewAccess`, `CheckAccessNotGranted`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain or grant specified permissions. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals that may be granted access to the resource. The check fails when the resource-based policy grants access beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for resource-based policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept on grants to an AWS service principal: one statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the policy grants a service principal access that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.AuthorizerConfiguration.CustomJWTAuthorizer.DiscoveryUrl`, the OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider that authenticates callers to your gateway through JWT-based inbound authorization, before provisioning. Requiring trusted OIDC identity providers helps prevent an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway that designates an untrusted provider from being provisioned.

This implementation guidance recommends validating, before provisioning, that `$.Tags{key}` declares owner and purpose tags. Requiring those tags helps prevent an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway that omits them from being provisioned and helps keep ownership and business function attributable.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.configuration.Tags{key}` on each Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway and flagging any that omit your required owner and purpose tag keys. Surfacing those resources helps you attribute each Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway to an accountable owner and the business function it supports.

This implementation guidance recommends restricting `bedrock-agentcore:CreateGateway` and `bedrock-agentcore:TagResource` with the `aws:RequestTag/owner`, `aws:RequestTag/purpose`, and `aws:TagKeys` condition keys in a service control policy (SCP). These conditions help prevent creating or tagging an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway without the owner and purpose tag keys, or removing them through `bedrock-agentcore:UntagResource`.

Use `aws:RequestTag/owner` and `aws:RequestTag/purpose` so that a request omitting either one is denied. Use `aws:TagKeys` to require each key in its exact case because the tag-key portion of `aws:RequestTag/tag-key` is not case-sensitive. Also use `aws:TagKeys` on the untag action so that a request removing either key is denied.

guidance.description:
When your gateway uses a `CUSTOM_JWT` authorizer with a private (VPC-hosted) identity provider, AgentCore reaches it through a private endpoint. With a managed VPC resource, AgentCore associates the security groups you list in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` with a VPC Lattice resource gateway in your VPC. If you don't specify any, the default security group for the VPC is used. That group's rules then govern traffic to your identity provider.

Configure these security groups following least-privilege best practices. Restrict inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. For this gateway, the required traffic is typically HTTPS on port 443 to your identity provider's OIDC discovery, JWKS, and token endpoints. Avoid rules that permit unrestricted access from or to any IP address (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0). Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. That peer can be your identity provider or an internal load balancer in front of it. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change. Apply the same least-privilege review to the security groups that govern any additional identity provider domains you configure in `privateEndpointOverrides`.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope each policy by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common policy applies a baseline group. A content audit policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow-list or block-list. It flags non-compliant groups in a central dashboard, notifies you, and can auto-remediate. Review its findings before you turn on automatic remediation. A usage audit policy removes unused or redundant groups. The managed resource gateway is read-only to you. Target the security groups you supply, for example with a content audit policy that covers Amazon VPC security groups.

To verify unintended access permitted by your security groups, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended. For example, match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. You can reference the security groups you supply by ID as a path source or destination. Create the scope with `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, start an analysis with `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer reasons about the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

links.title: Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager
How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends restricting the inbound and outbound rules on the security groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]`, the groups on the VPC Lattice resource gateway that carries traffic to your identity provider, to the required addresses, protocols, and ports. Excluding unrestricted addresses such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 from those inbound and outbound rules helps reduce the network exposure of your gateway's identity provider private endpoint.

This implementation guidance recommends validating the inbound and outbound rules of the security groups resolved from `$.AuthorizerConfiguration.CustomJWTAuthorizer.PrivateEndpoint.ManagedVpcResource.SecurityGroupIds[*]` before provisioning. Checking for rules that allow any address on unintended ports, directly or through a prefix list, helps prevent an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway from being provisioned with such groups.

This implementation guidance recommends resolving the security groups recorded at `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` and `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpointOverrides[*].privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` and inspecting their inbound and outbound rules. Flagging rules that admit 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 on sensitive ports, broad port ranges, or all protocols helps you detect your gateways' identity provider private endpoints with broader network exposure than they need.

This implementation guidance recommends recording the CloudWatch Logs operations that can disable or weaken the vended logs delivery for your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway. Recording calls such as `DeleteDelivery`, `DeleteLogGroup`, and `PutRetentionPolicy`, together with the calling identity, helps you detect and attribute those changes.

This implementation guidance recommends flagging an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway with no vended logs delivery to CloudWatch Logs, read from `$.deliveries[*].deliveryDestinationType`, the delivery's destination type. Surfacing that gap helps you detect gateway request and tool invocation activity that is not being recorded for review.

This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.PrivateEndpoint.ManagedVpcResource.SubnetIds[*]`, the subnets hosting the managed resource gateway, by resolving each subnet's route table for a default route to an internet gateway before provisioning. Subnets carrying that route fail validation, which helps prevent an AgentCore Gateway target's private endpoint from being provisioned in a public subnet.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`, the managed resource gateway's subnet IDs, then resolving each subnet's route table. Flagging a gateway target with a subnet whose default route targets an internet gateway, read at `$.RouteTables[*].Routes[*].GatewayId`, helps you detect placement in a public subnet.

This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.PrivateEndpoint.ManagedVpcResource.SubnetIds[*]`, the managed private endpoint's subnets, or `$.PrivateEndpoint.SelfManagedLatticeResource.ResourceConfigurationIdentifier`, your self-managed VPC Lattice resource configuration, before provisioning. That check helps prevent an AgentCore Gateway target from being provisioned without that VPC configuration, so its traffic can traverse your VPC subnets under your security groups.

This implementation guidance recommends flagging gateway targets whose `$.configuration.PrivateEndpoint`, the private endpoint configuration, is absent. Surfacing them helps you detect gateway targets that run without a private VPC Lattice path into your VPC.

This implementation guidance recommends applying the `bedrock-agentcore:PrivateEndpointType` condition key in a service control policy (SCP) to govern `bedrock-agentcore:CreateGatewayTarget` and `bedrock-agentcore:UpdateGatewayTarget`. This condition helps prevent principals in your organization from deploying Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway targets without a private endpoint into an Amazon VPC.

guidance.description:
For gateway targets that use a managed private endpoint, supply two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`. Set this list when you call `CreateGatewayTarget` or `UpdateGatewayTarget`. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore places the target's managed VPC Lattice resource gateway in those subnets. The resource gateway is a wrapper around elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in your VPC. Each subnet resides in a single Availability Zone. A one-subnet list therefore puts every interface in the same zone. Spreading the ENIs across zones helps your target's private connectivity survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

Subnet-to-zone membership is a property of each subnet, not of the gateway target. Before you supply subnet IDs, call `DescribeSubnets` and confirm from the `AvailabilityZone` field that the subnets belong to distinct Availability Zones. Also confirm from the `AvailabilityZoneId` field that each subnet is in a zone that AgentCore Gateway supports for managed private endpoints in your Region. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review for the templates and modules that create your gateway targets. Each review should confirm that the template supplies at least two subnets from different zones. In AWS CloudFormation, this list is the `SubnetIds` property of `ManagedVpcResource` in an `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::GatewayTarget` resource.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetGatewayTarget`. The response echoes the configured subnets and returns the ARN of the managed resource gateway. Confirm that those subnets span more than one Availability Zone. You can also list the resource gateway's network interfaces with `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` and confirm that their subnets span more than one zone.

To assess and track Availability Zone resilience at scale, use AWS Resilience Hub. Add your application's resources to a Resilience Hub application and run a resiliency assessment. The assessment measures resiliency against the targets your resiliency policy sets for Availability Zone disruptions. Coverage depends on the resource types that Resilience Hub supports. Where it does not assess your gateway target directly, include the supported resources behind your private endpoint. Examples include an internal load balancer, a private Amazon API Gateway API, or backend compute.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`, the subnets of your gateway target's managed private endpoint. Spreading the network interfaces AgentCore creates for the endpoint's VPC Lattice resource gateway across zones helps private connectivity survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

This implementation guidance recommends validating, before provisioning, that `$.PrivateEndpoint.ManagedVpcResource.SubnetIds[*]`, your gateway target's VPC subnets, lists two or more subnet entries. That check helps prevent a single-subnet gateway target from being provisioned, so its private endpoint's network interfaces can span more than one Availability Zone.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.configuration.PrivateEndpoint`, the private endpoint setting that lists your target's resource gateway subnets, then resolving each subnet's Availability Zone. Flagging a gateway target with a managed private endpoint confined to a single Availability Zone helps you detect the target's resource gateway network interfaces that lack multi-zone redundancy.

This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.TargetConfiguration.Mcp.McpServer.Endpoint` (the MCP server endpoint), `$.TargetConfiguration.Http.Passthrough.Endpoint` (the passthrough endpoint), `$.TargetConfiguration.Inference.Provider.Endpoint` (the inference provider endpoint), and `$.TargetConfiguration.Mcp.OpenApiSchema.InlinePayload` or `$.TargetConfiguration.Mcp.OpenApiSchema.S3.Uri` (the inline or Amazon S3-hosted OpenAPI schema whose server URL the gateway calls) before provisioning. That check helps prevent an AgentCore Gateway target from being provisioned with an HTTP endpoint outside your organization's trust boundary.

As part of your data perimeter, CloudFormation Hooks can help prevent developers from specifying gateway target configurations that do not belong to your organization. This guide applies that check to each HTTP endpoint the target configuration carries, such as `$.TargetConfiguration.Http.Passthrough.Endpoint`, the passthrough endpoint.

This implementation guidance recommends recording `CreateGatewayTarget` and `UpdateGatewayTarget` calls together with `$.targetConfiguration.mcp.mcpServer.endpoint` (the MCP server endpoint), `$.targetConfiguration.http.passthrough.endpoint` (the HTTP passthrough endpoint), `$.targetConfiguration.inference.provider.endpoint` (the inference provider endpoint), `$.targetConfiguration.mcp.openApiSchema.inlinePayload` (the inline OpenAPI schema whose server URL sets the endpoint), and `$.targetConfiguration.mcp.openApiSchema.s3.uri` (the Amazon S3 location of that schema). Recording those calls helps you detect a gateway target configured with an HTTP endpoint URL outside your organization, to which it forwards tool calls, agent traffic, and model requests with any outbound credentials the gateway injects.

Recording the `targetConfiguration` request parameter of `CreateGatewayTarget` and `UpdateGatewayTarget` calls helps you verify that your gateway targets reach only endpoints within your organization's trust boundary. This monitoring complements your resource perimeter, because the calls the gateway makes to a configured endpoint can fall outside your permissions guardrails. When a recorded endpoint points to a resource outside your organization, remediate with the responsive controls of your choice.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.targetConfiguration.mcp.mcpServer.endpoint` (the MCP server endpoint), `$.targetConfiguration.http.passthrough.endpoint` (the HTTP passthrough endpoint), `$.targetConfiguration.inference.provider.endpoint` (the inference provider endpoint), and `$.targetConfiguration.mcp.openApiSchema.inlinePayload` (the inline OpenAPI schema that holds the server URL) recorded on each gateway target. Flagging a target HTTP endpoint you have not designated as trusted helps you detect delivery of gateway requests and any injected credentials to endpoints outside your trust boundary.

guidance.description:
Follow least-privilege best practices for the security groups that you specify in `$.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` when you call `CreateGatewayTarget` or `UpdateGatewayTarget`. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore associates these groups with the managed VPC Lattice resource gateway that it places in your subnets. Their outbound rules control traffic from the resource gateway to your private resource, such as an MCP server or REST API. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. For example, allow outbound traffic only to your private resource on the port that it listens on, typically 443 for HTTPS. If you route traffic through an intermediate domain, such as a VPC endpoint or internal load balancer, allow traffic to that component instead. Avoid rules that permit unrestricted access from or to any address, such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change. If you don't specify any security groups, AgentCore uses the default security group for the VPC. Its default rules allow all outbound IPv4 traffic, plus IPv6 traffic when the VPC has an IPv6 CIDR block. Specify security groups with restricted rules instead of relying on the default security group.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope these policies by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group. It flags noncompliant groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can automatically remediate noncompliant rules. A usage audit security group policy identifies unused or redundant security groups and can remove them. You can't modify the managed resource gateway. Policy actions that change its security group associations might not apply to it. Content audit policies can still evaluate the rules in the security groups that you create and specify. Review the findings before you enable automatic remediation. Automatic remediation can remove a rule that the connection to your private resource requires.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access that you consider unintended. For a gateway target, you can also match paths that start at the resource gateway's security groups and exclude paths that end at your private resource.
