guidance.description:
By default, a harness runs on the public network. When you deploy the harness in your VPC with network mode `VPC`, supply two or more subnets that resolve to different Availability Zones. Set them in `$.environment.agentCoreRuntimeEnvironment.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.subnets[*]` in your `CreateHarness` and `UpdateHarness` requests. AgentCore creates the elastic network interfaces (ENIs) for your harness's managed AgentCore Runtime in the subnets you specify. Subnets in different zones let AgentCore place those ENIs in more than one Availability Zone. This helps your harness keep VPC connectivity through the loss of a single zone. The subnet list accepts a single subnet, so multi-AZ placement depends on the subnets you supply. If your inbound JWT authorizer reaches a private identity provider through a managed VPC resource, apply the same practice to `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`. AgentCore Identity places the ENIs of its managed VPC Lattice resource gateway in those subnets.

Each subnet belongs to one Availability Zone, so the zones your harness uses depend on the subnets you choose. Before you supply subnet IDs, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation and confirm that they belong to distinct Availability Zones. Check the `AvailabilityZone` and `AvailabilityZoneId` response fields. Also confirm that each Availability Zone ID is one that AgentCore supports for VPC connectivity in your Region. Subnets in unsupported Availability Zones cause resource creation to fail. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so that the templates and modules that create harnesses supply at least two subnets from different Availability Zones. This review includes templates that declare `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Harness` resources. If your harness mounts Amazon EFS or Amazon S3 Files access points, create a mount target in each Availability Zone that your harness subnets use. Sessions placed in a zone without a mount target can fail to mount the file system.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetHarness` and resolve the subnets in its runtime network configuration with `DescribeSubnets`. Confirm that those subnets span more than one Availability Zone. Then list the network interfaces in those subnets with the Amazon EC2 `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` operation. Confirm that the attached ENIs exist in more than one Availability Zone. AgentCore shares ENIs across agents that use the same subnet and security group configuration. An interface you find might therefore also serve other agents.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, use AWS Resilience Hub. Include your harness's application resources in a Resilience Hub application and run a resiliency assessment. The assessment can flag single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is not among the services on the Resilience Hub list of supported resources. An assessment might therefore evaluate only the supported resources your harness depends on, such as Amazon EFS file systems, NAT gateways, and databases. Continue to verify your harness's own subnet placement directly.

guidance.description:
Configure the security groups that govern your harness's network traffic following least-privilege best practices. In VPC network mode, AgentCore attaches the groups in `$.environment.agentCoreRuntimeEnvironment.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.securityGroups[*]` to the elastic network interfaces it creates in your subnets for harness sessions. These groups govern the traffic your sessions send to VPC resources, AWS service endpoints, and the internet. When your inbound JWT authorizer uses a managed private endpoint, the groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` attach to its VPC Lattice resource gateway. That resource gateway carries authorizer traffic to your private identity provider.

Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. Harness sessions run on a managed AgentCore Runtime that initiates outbound connections. The session groups generally need no inbound rules. Replace the default outbound rule that allows all traffic with rules for the destinations your harness uses. For example, allow HTTPS to the security groups of your Amazon ECR and Amazon Bedrock runtime interface endpoints. Allow HTTPS to the Amazon S3 prefix list for your gateway endpoint. Allow only your database port, such as TCP 3306, to a database's security group. Allow only TCP 2049 to the security groups of file system mount targets. Limit internet egress for Git skills, remote MCP servers, or public container image pulls to the required ports and, where known, address ranges. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change. For the authorizer's resource gateway, allow outbound traffic only to your identity provider endpoint on the protocol and port it listens on. If you omit those groups, the default security group for the VPC is used. Specify dedicated groups instead. Avoid rules that permit 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, particularly on administrative or sensitive ports. Rule changes apply automatically to every resource that uses a group. Review the groups themselves, not only the harness configuration.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope each policy by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common policy applies a baseline security group. A content audit policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or block list. It flags noncompliant groups in a central dashboard, can notify you, and can remediate them automatically. A usage audit policy identifies unused or redundant groups and can remove or consolidate them. To focus a content audit policy, tag the security groups your harnesses use and scope the policy to that tag. AgentCore creates and manages harness network interfaces through a service-linked role. Firewall Manager can't update security groups on requester-managed network interfaces. Confirm how a common policy treats these interfaces before you rely on it. A usage audit policy may treat a group that your harness configuration references as unused when no network interface currently uses it. Review policy findings before you enable automatic remediation.

To verify unintended access permitted by your security groups, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended. For example, match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. You can also match paths from your harness security groups to an internet gateway and exclude the ports you require. Create the scope with `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, run it with `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer reasons about the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

When you configure a managed private endpoint on an OAuth2 credential provider, supply two or more subnets that resolve to different Availability Zones. Private endpoints are configured in the custom provider configuration (`customOauth2ProviderConfig`). Set the subnets in `privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds` when you call `CreateOauth2CredentialProvider` or `UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider`. Apply the same rule to each `privateEndpointOverrides` entry that uses a managed VPC resource. AgentCore Identity places its managed VPC Lattice resource gateway in these subnets. The gateway's elastic network interfaces (ENIs) carry traffic to your VPC-hosted identity provider. Placing those interfaces in more than one Availability Zone helps that connectivity survive the loss of a single zone.

Subnet-to-AZ membership is a property of each subnet, not of the credential provider. Before you supply subnet IDs, call Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` and use the `AvailabilityZone` response field to confirm that they belong to distinct Availability Zones. Each subnet also needs network access to your identity provider's discovery and token endpoints. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so that the templates and modules that create `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OAuth2CredentialProvider` resources supply at least two subnets from different Availability Zones.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetOauth2CredentialProvider` and review the subnet IDs returned in the custom provider's private endpoint configuration. Then enumerate the resource gateway's network interfaces with Amazon EC2 `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` and confirm that their subnets span more than one Availability Zone. The managed resource gateway is read-only to you. To change its zones, update the subnet list on the credential provider. `UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider` requires the vendor and the full provider configuration.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, use AWS Resilience Hub. Include your application's resources in a Resilience Hub application and run a resiliency assessment, which can flag single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. The list of resources that Resilience Hub supports does not include Amazon Bedrock AgentCore or Amazon VPC Lattice. Use it for the supported resources in your application, such as those that host your identity provider, alongside the subnet and network interface checks above.

guidance.description:
Configure the security groups for your OAuth2 credential provider's private endpoint by following least-privilege best practices. These are the security groups that you list in `$.oauth2ProviderConfigInput.customOauth2ProviderConfig.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` for a custom OAuth2 provider. They also include the groups in each per-domain `privateEndpointOverrides[*].privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` entry. You set them when you call `CreateOauth2CredentialProvider` or `UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider`. AgentCore Identity associates them with the VPC Lattice resource gateway that it creates and manages in your subnets. Their outbound rules control the traffic that the resource gateway sends to your identity provider's discovery and token endpoints. If you specify no security groups, the default security group for the VPC is used. That group's default rules allow all outbound traffic and inbound traffic from resources assigned to the same group. Specify custom security groups for the private endpoint instead, and avoid rules that allow unrestricted traffic from or to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. For example, allow outbound HTTPS only on the port that your identity provider uses, typically 443, and only to its endpoints. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope these policies by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group to in-scope resources. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or a block list. It flags noncompliant security groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can automatically remediate noncompliant rules. A usage audit security group policy can remove unused or redundant security groups.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access that you consider unintended. For example, the scope might match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. Create the scope with `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, run an analysis with `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer evaluates the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP address assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

When your payment manager uses a custom JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer with a managed private endpoint, supply two or more subnets from different Availability Zones (AZs). Set them in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` when you call `CreatePaymentManager` or `UpdatePaymentManager`. AgentCore creates and manages a VPC Lattice resource gateway for your private identity provider and places it in those subnets. The resource gateway is built from elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in the listed subnets, so the subnets' AZs decide where those ENIs reside. Spreading the ENIs across AZs helps AgentCore keep reaching your identity provider's discovery and JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) endpoints if a single AZ is lost. Choose only subnets that can reach those endpoints.

Then run a resiliency assessment, which flags single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. Resilience Hub assesses only the resource types it supports. guidance.description:
Apply least-privilege rules to the security groups for your payment manager's managed private endpoint. You can name up to five groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` when you call `CreatePaymentManager` or `UpdatePaymentManager`. AgentCore attaches them to the VPC Lattice resource gateway it creates in your VPC to reach your private identity provider's OIDC discovery and JWKS endpoints. Their rules control the traffic that the gateway's network interfaces send to your identity provider. If you don't name any groups, the VPC's default security group is used, so review its rules as well. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the sources and destinations you need (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports, such as HTTPS to your identity provider's endpoints. Don't allow unrestricted access from or to any IP address (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0). If the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, such as an internal Application Load Balancer in front of your identity provider, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations, scoped by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or block list. It flags noncompliant groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can remediate them automatically. You can include the Amazon VPC security group resource type in a content audit policy's scope, which brings the groups you name for the private endpoint into scope directly. A usage audit security group policy removes unused or redundant security groups.

To check for unintended access that your security groups allow, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope (`CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`) for the access that you consider unintended, for example any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. Then run an analysis (`StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`) and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer evaluates the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment to find network access that doesn't match your security and compliance requirements.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends restricting the inbound and outbound rules on the security groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]`, the groups associated with your payment manager's managed VPC Lattice resource gateway, to the required addresses, protocols, and ports. Excluding unrestricted addresses such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 from those inbound and outbound rules helps reduce the network exposure of the resource gateway's network interfaces.

This implementation guidance recommends resolving the security groups recorded at `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` and inspecting their inbound and outbound rules. Flagging rules that admit 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 on sensitive ports, broad port ranges, or all protocols helps you detect your managed VPC Lattice resource gateways with broader network exposure than they need.

This implementation guidance recommends recording the CloudWatch Logs operations that can disable or weaken the vended logs delivery for your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payment manager. Recording calls such as `DeleteDelivery`, `DeleteDeliverySource`, and `PutRetentionPolicy`, together with the calling identity, helps you detect and attribute those changes.

This implementation guidance recommends flagging an AgentCore payment manager with no vended logs delivery to CloudWatch Logs, read from `$.deliveries[*].deliveryDestinationType`, the delivery's destination type. Surfacing that gap helps you detect AgentCore payments data plane API activity that is not being recorded for review.

This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.EncryptionKeyArn`, the AWS KMS key that encrypts your policy engine and its policies, before provisioning. Requiring a customer managed key in your account, with key material that is neither imported nor held in an external key store, helps prevent an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policy engine from being provisioned without a key whose policy, lifecycle, and key material you control.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.policyEngines[*].encryptionKeyArn`, the AWS KMS key that encrypts each policy engine and its policies, and resolving `$.KeyMetadata.KeyManager`, `$.KeyMetadata.AWSAccountId`, and `$.KeyMetadata.Origin` for that key. Flagging Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policy engines whose key is not a customer managed key in your account, or whose key material is imported or held in an external key store, helps you detect where you do not control the key policy, lifecycle, or key material.

This implementation guidance recommends validating, before provisioning, that `$.Tags[*].Key` and `$.Tags[*].Value` declare owner and purpose tags. Requiring those tags helps prevent an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policy engine that omits them from being provisioned and helps keep ownership and business function attributable.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.tags{key}` on each AgentCore policy engine listed through `$.policyEngines[*].policyEngineArn` and flagging any that omit your required owner and purpose tag keys. Surfacing those resources helps you attribute each AgentCore policy engine to an accountable owner and the business function it supports.

This implementation guidance recommends restricting `bedrock-agentcore:CreatePolicyEngine` and `bedrock-agentcore:TagResource` with the `aws:RequestTag/owner`, `aws:RequestTag/purpose`, and `aws:TagKeys` condition keys in a service control policy (SCP). These conditions help prevent creating or tagging an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policy engine without the owner and purpose tag keys, or removing them through `bedrock-agentcore:UntagResource`.

Use `aws:RequestTag/owner` and `aws:RequestTag/purpose` so that a request omitting either one is denied. Use `aws:TagKeys` to require each key in its exact case because the tag-key portion of `aws:RequestTag/tag-key` is not case-sensitive. Also use `aws:TagKeys` on the untag action so that a request removing either key is denied.

This implementation guidance recommends flagging a registry whose `$.registries[*].authorizerType`, the authorizer type for consumer search and MCP endpoint access, is `CUSTOM_JWT` rather than `AWS_IAM`. Flagging these registries helps you detect where callers with your identity provider's bearer tokens can be granted `bedrock-agentcore:SearchRegistryRecords` and `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeRegistryMcp` access without IAM authorization.

guidance.description:
When your registry uses the `CUSTOM_JWT` authorizer with a managed private endpoint to reach an identity provider hosted in your VPC, supply two or more subnets that resolve to different Availability Zones. Set these subnets in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` when you call `CreateRegistry`, or in `$.authorizerConfiguration.optionalValue.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` when you call `UpdateRegistry`. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore places the network interfaces of the VPC Lattice resource gateway that it manages on your behalf in the subnets that you list. Spreading those subnets across zones places network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone. This helps your registry's private connectivity to the identity provider's OIDC discovery and JWKS endpoints survive the loss of a single zone. Choose only subnets from which those identity provider endpoints are reachable. Changing the authorizer configuration can disrupt existing consumers of a registry, so plan subnet changes on a registry that is in use.

Subnet-to-Availability Zone membership is a property of each subnet, not of the registry. Before you supply subnet IDs, use the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation to confirm from the `AvailabilityZone` field that the chosen subnets belong to distinct Availability Zones. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code and automation review so that the templates, modules, and scripts that call `CreateRegistry` or `UpdateRegistry` supply at least two subnets from different Availability Zones.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetRegistry` and review the managed private endpoint subnet IDs in the returned authorizer configuration. Then use the Amazon EC2 `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` operation to enumerate the network interfaces in those subnets. Confirm that the resource gateway's network interfaces span more than one Availability Zone.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, include the application resources around your registry, such as the resources that host your identity provider, in an AWS Resilience Hub application. Then run a resiliency assessment, which flags single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. Resilience Hub assesses only the resource types that it supports, so confirm which of your resources it can assess.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`, the subnet IDs of your registry's managed private endpoint. Spreading the network interfaces of the AgentCore-managed VPC Lattice resource gateway across zones helps private connectivity to your identity provider survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`, the subnets where your registry's managed VPC Lattice resource gateway is placed, then resolving each subnet's Availability Zone. Flagging a registry with a managed private endpoint confined to a single Availability Zone helps you detect its resource gateway network interfaces that lack multi-zone redundancy.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl`, the OpenID Connect discovery URL of the identity provider that authenticates consumers to your registry's search API and MCP endpoint. Flagging an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore registry whose recorded provider you do not trust helps you detect an authentication path that could allow unintended access.

guidance.description:
If your registry's custom JWT authorizer uses a managed private endpoint, AgentCore creates and manages a VPC Lattice resource gateway in your VPC. Its network interfaces carry the registry's traffic to your identity provider's discovery and JWKS endpoints. You associate security groups with it through `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` on `CreateRegistry`, or its `optionalValue` counterpart on `UpdateRegistry`. If you don't specify any, the VPC's default security group is associated.

Configure these security groups following least-privilege best practices. Restrict inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. Outbound rules on a resource gateway's security groups control its traffic to your identity provider. Your identity provider typically uses port 443 for HTTPS. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. For example, reference your identity provider's security group in the resource gateway's outbound rules. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope these policies by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or a block list. It flags noncompliant security groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can automatically remediate noncompliant rules. A usage audit security group policy removes unused or redundant security groups. Content audit policies can scope Amazon VPC security groups directly. That scope includes the security groups you create and associate with the AgentCore-managed resource gateway.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended. For example, match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. Create the scope by calling `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, then run an analysis by calling `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis` and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer evaluates your security groups together with route tables, network ACLs, and public IP assignments. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.synchronizationConfiguration.fromUrl.credentialProviderConfigurations[*].credentialProvider.iamCredentialProvider.roleArn`, your registry record's sync role, then evaluating `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`, that role's trust policy, with IAM Access Analyzer. Flagging trust policies that allow public role assumption, or assumption beyond your reference policy, or that omit the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, helps you detect overly permissive role assumption.

This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends a trust policy that restricts assumption of your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore registry record's sync role, `$.synchronizationConfiguration.fromUrl.credentialProviderConfigurations[*].credentialProvider.iamCredentialProvider.roleArn` and `$.synchronizationConfiguration.optionalValue.fromUrl.credentialProviderConfigurations[*].credentialProvider.iamCredentialProvider.roleArn`, to the `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com` service principal.

Confirm that IAM role trust policies grant access only to the AWS service principals you intend. Review the `Principal` element of each policy and verify it names only the service principals your workload requires.

This implementation guidance recommends restricting `sts:AssumeRole` with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key in a resource control policy (RCP), while exempting AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) and scoping those service requests with `aws:SourceOrgID`. These conditions help prevent principals outside your organization from assuming your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore registry record's sync role, `$.synchronizationConfiguration.fromUrl.credentialProviderConfigurations[*].credentialProvider.iamCredentialProvider.roleArn` and `$.synchronizationConfiguration.optionalValue.fromUrl.credentialProviderConfigurations[*].credentialProvider.iamCredentialProvider.roleArn`.

To restrict access to trusted identities, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys to restrict service access to your roles. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.
